speechtext:
The house resumed from Friday, March 24, consideration in committee of Bill No. 21, to amend the Indian Act-Mr. Murphy.-Mr. Gagnon in the chair.
On section 7-Enquiry as to fitness for enfranchisement.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to
make a few remarks concerning the Six Nations Indians. These Indians are not natives of Canada, as we understand the term. At the time of the discovery of America, or at least shortly afterwards, these Indians were settled in the Mohawk valley in the state of New York. As they are not natives of Canada, in the same sense as other Indians, I claim and they claim that they are in a class by themselves. Readers of history will remember that during the revolutionary war these Indians were allies of the British government and while that war turned out so disastrously for the British army, +hey remained loyal to the British Empii-o Subsequently, by virtue of what is known as the Haldimand treaty, they were allowed to come over to Canada. The Haldimand tre&jy, so-called, is very short and I think I cannot do better than read the material portions of it. It is dated October 25, 1784, and recites:
Whereas His Majesty having been pleased to direct that, in consideration of the early attachment to his cause manifested by the Mohawk
Indians and of the loss of their settlement which they thereby sustained a convenient tract of land under his protection should be chosen as a safe and comfortable retreat for them and others of the Six Nations who have either lost their settlements within the territory of the American states or wish to retire from them to the British. I have at the earnest desire of many of these His Majesty's faithful allies purchased a tract of land from the Indians situated between the lakes Ontario, Erie and Huron, and I do hereby in His Majesty's name authorize and permit the said Mohawk nation and such others of the Six Nation Indians as wish to settle in that quarter to take possession of and settle upon the banks of the river commonly called Ouse or Grand river, running into lake Erie, allotting to them for that purpose six miles deep from each side of the river, beginning at lake Erie and extending in that proportion to the head of the said river which they and their posterity are to enjoy forever.
Given under my hand and seal at arms-
In pursuance of that treaty the Six Nations Indians, or the greater bulk of them, came over from New York state where they had been living, and settled in the western part of Ontario. The British government had not at that time acquired all the land which they had agreed to give to the Six Nations Indians, but they afterwards by treaty acquired the land from the Mississauga Indians and subsequently made good their agreement to allow the Six Nations Indians to settle in that portion of western Ontario.
Following that treaty, what is known as the Simcoe deed was entered into pursuant to the Haldimand treaty. I want to read the material parts of the Simcoe deed, which is dated January 14, 1793:
Know ye, that whereas the attachment and fidelity of the chiefs, warriors, and people of the Six Nations, to us and our government has been made manifest on divers occasions by their spirited and zealous exertions and by the bravery of their conduct, and we being desirous of showing our approbation of the same and in recompense of the losses they may have sustained of providing a convenient tract of land under our protection for a safe and suitable retreat for them and their posterity, have of our special grace, certain knowledge and mere motion, given and granted-
This is a deed; Governor Simcoe, representing the king has given and granted this land.
-and by these presents do give and grant to the chiefs, warriors, women and people of the said Six Nations and their heirs forever, all that district or territory of land-
And so forth, described as I have given it before.
Giving and granting, and by these presents confirming to the said chiefs, warriors, women
Indian Act

and people of the said Six Nations and their heirs, the full and entire possession, use, benefit and advantage of the said district or territory, to be held and enjoyed by them in the most free and ample manner, and according to the several customs and usages of them the said chiefs, warriors, women and people of the said Six Nations; provided always, and be it understood to be the true intent and meaning of these presents that, for the purpose of assuring the said lands, as aforesaid to the said chiefs, warriors, women and people of the Six Nations, and their heirs, and of securing to them the free and undisturbed possession and enjoyment of the same, it is^ our royal will and pleasure that no transfer, alienation, conveyance, sale, gift, exchange, lease, property or possession, shall at any time be had, made or given of the said district or territory, or any part or parcel thereof, by any of the said chiefs, warriors, women or people, to any other nation or body of people, person or persons whatever, other than among themselves the said chiefs, warriors, women and people, but that any such transfer, alienation, conveyance, sale, gift, exchange, lease or possession, shall be null and void, and of no effect whatever, and that no person or persons shall possess or occupy the said district or territory or any part or parcel thereof, by or under any pretence or any such alienation, title or conveyance, as aforesaid, or by or under any pretence whatever, under pain of our severe displeasure.
And so on. That, as I say, places the band of Indians known as the Six Nations in an altogether different category from other Indians in this country. I want to call the attention of the .committee to the definition of the word " band " in the interpretation clause of the Indian Act. Section 2, paragraph (b) reads:
"Band" means any tribe, band or body of Indians who own or are interested in a reserve-
This is not a reserve at all.
-or in Indian lands in common, of which the legal title is vested in the crown.
The legal title to those lands is not vested in the crown because, according to the Simcoe deed which I have read, it is granted, to the Six Nations Indians, so that the word "band" does not apply to the Six Nations Indians.
We find the term "reserve" defined in paragraph (j) which reads:
"Reserve" means any tract or tracts of land set apart by treaty or otherwise for the use or benefit of or granted to a particular band of Indians, of which the legal title is in the crown.
Those are the same words used there. I claim that the legal title to those lands is not in the crown and therefore the present Indian Act should not be held to be applicable to the Six Nations Indians.

Let us refer again to the history of the Six Nations Indians. In the war of 1812-14 we find that they took the side of the British in fighting against the Americans. In the rebellion of 1837 they took the part of the loyal citizens of Canada of that day in fighting the battles of Great Britain. Then in the great war I can only refer to a speech made by a former Minister of the Interior in this house when he said that 600 of the Indians of the Six Nations volunteered to fight in the great war. Let us understand what 600 means in comparison with the small number of that whole Indian band, which does not comprise more than 4,000 or 5,000 people, including men, women and children. When one thinks 600 of their men of military age volunteered for service in the great war, surely one realizes that we in considering this bill in Canada owe some recognition of their sacrifices.	.
By the way, I understand an amendment has been proposed. I am told the legal department of the government hold that the Haldimand treaty is not a treaty, therefore the exception in this bill will not provide the remedy or help out the Six Nations Indians in their present claim. But reading the Haldimand treaty with the Simcoe deed, one cannot come to any other conclusion than that those lands belong to the Six Nations Indians and are to be held by them according to their ancient customs. I should like, if I may, to read a copy of a letter which I received and which was sent to the press, signed by W. F. Powless, who is secretary of the Six Nations council. This letter, which is dated March 11, 1933, reads:
Sir,-Allow me to give you an explanation of the objections and contentions of the Six Nations Indians with regard to the enfranchisement clause of the Indian Act now under discussion in the House of Commons, Ottawa, and of which there appears to be such little interest shown in a matter that is of vital interest to us and which threatens our very existence.
The part of the act dealing with the enfranchisement of Indians has been a matter of concern by succeeding governments, with the object in view of forcing full citizenship on a people the large majority of whom have not as yet attained that point where it would be to their advantage to be placed in business competition with the surrounding whites.
Only two or three generations ago their ancestors obtained their livelihood by the hunt having no knowledge of any other method while the whites have had hundreds of years of experience both in business and the art of farming and now the government is endeavouring to force compulsory enfranchisement on the Indian which we consider is one of the most

Indian Act
vicious pieces of legislation ever enacted. True, there are among the Indians of Canada, outstanding men and women who have obtained a prominent place in both the literary and professional world but they are in a very small minority and the Indians are urging that there be a distinction shown and that the proposed amendment to the act relative to the compulsory enfranchisement of Indians, empowering a body of men to decide as to the fitness of an Indian of a band to take the responsibility of full citizenship without first consulting the party or parties most interested, should not be allowed to become law.
There is a feeling of discouragement among the Indians and a suspicion of the motives of the government in the measure under discussion and as long as there is no satisfactory assurance that they will remain unmolested on their reserves there will be a tendency to neglect improvements on their farms as they contend that they have no guarantee that their children will be able to enjoy the fruits of their industry.
The Six Nations, in the short time that they have taken up farming, have become entirely self supporting and I venture to say that there is less destitution on their reserve at the present time than in any other community in Canada, being less than 10 per cent of the population. This is of course not generally known but what is known among a certain class of whites and of which they take full advantage is that the Indian has not the business ability to compete with his white neighbour.
True, we have been assured that the government has no designs on the Six Nations reserve but the amendment, if passed, will confer the power and may be exercised by a succeeding government if it so desires.
Another matter that should not be lost sight of is the magnificent response made by the Indians in practically every war in which the empire has been engaged in in the last 160 years and particularly in the great war when there was a larger percentage of voluntary enlistments from them than from any other class in Canada. And what is the thanks extended to the Indian returned veterans for their sacrifice? The benefits of relief to small pensioners have been passed to the Department of Indian Affairs while participation in the Cast Post fund has been entirely withdrawn although they helped to accumulate the profits derived from canteen funds and were asked to vote on the question of the disposition of said profits.
In conclusion I would appeal to the fair minded people of Canada, who have the interest of the Indian at heart, to make representations to the government urging that the proposed amendment be withdrawn. If that is done and the objectionable measure dropped they will win the everlasting gratitude of a people who never forget a kindness done them.
The Simcoe deed included all the territory from lake Erie along the Grand river, six miles on either side from mouth to source. As the years went on the Six Nations found that they could not usefully occupy the whole of that territory, and from time to time they surrendered certain portions to the crown, and now they occupy all of the township of Tuscarora, part of Onondaga and part of the township of Oneida in the adjoining county of Haldimand. The moneys paid into the Indian office in England, Indian affairs in Canada for several years having been administered in London, for the surrender of these important blocks of land are supposed to be lying somewhere down here in the treasury at Ottawa. The sum in the first place was very close to one million dollars but it has been depleted from one cause or another. I am not complaining of that depletion except with regard to one item, with respect to which I perhaps cannot do better than quote from a return that was passed by the house in 1927, and which is sessional paper 143. It says:
The only loss which was sustained by the Six Nations fund was owing to the unfortunate investment by the British Indian office of thirty-eight thousand pounds provicial currency in the Grand Kiver Navigation Company.
That was trust money which never should have been so invested. I have been told that over many years there have been applications sent in to this government and to the British government for a refund of that money. Being trust money it was misappropriated. The British government say:	Oh well, we handed
the whole thing over to Canada in 1867. The Canadian government say:	We did not do
it at all; it was done before we got hold of it. So they pass the buck from one to the other. That thirty-eight thousand pounds should be restored to the Six Nations Indian fund, although I must confess that the Six Nations Indians have almost given up hope that that will ever be done. I am told that the department claims that it has made that amount good to the Six Nations in various ways. The department has built a splendid hospital in Ohsweken in the county of Brant, and has built schools for the education of the Indians. But that same thing is done for the Indians throughout the whole dominion. It is the duty of the dominion government to do that, and for the department to say, "Oh, we have built hospitals and schools for the Indians of the Six Nations," when they do the same thing for Indians throughout this dominion is to put forward a contention in which I cannot see any merit at all.
I have obtained a copy of sessional paper 106 dated Friday, October 7, 1932, giving a list of the Indians enfranchised under the Indian Act for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1932. I find that from one end of Canada to the other there were only fifty-seven Indians granted enfranchisement during that year, and how many were there enfranchised among the Six Nations? Not one. They do not want it. Why then should legislation be passed amend-
Indian Act

ing the Indian Act and compelling their enfranchisement against their will provided that somebody decides that they are fit for enfranchisement? They do not want it, and are not asking for it.
The minister says that this government does not intend to enforce enfranchisement. If that is the case, why take this power and deprive the Indians of a good legal argument should the present government or any government in the future change the present policy and decide to enfranchise the Indians?
I think that an exception should be made of the Six Nations Indians, and I would offer an amendment for the consideration of the minister, that nothing in that particular section of the act shall apply to the Six Nations Indians of the Grand river.
I want again to refer to what the Six Nations Indians have done for the empire, and in that connection I cannot do better than quote a few lines from John McCrae's poem, In Flander's Fields. If justice is not done to the Six Nations Indians in this matter, I would ask if the government will not be in a similar position to that suggested in the last line of the poem:
We shall not sleep though poppies grow In Flanders fields.
I appeal to the minister to do everything possible, and there is a lot possible, to relieve the Indians of the Six Nations of the necessity of being enfranchised against their will.

Mr. Chairman, as the
previous speaker has said, the amendment to the Indian Act which is now being considered in committee, has been considered on former occasions. There still seems to be a misapprehension in regard to the bill before us. During the years the government of Canada has, I believe, quite properly taken a very liberal attitude towards the treatment of Indian residents in Canada. Literally millions of dollars have been spent for a certain fixed definite purpose-at least so it seems to me. Money has been spent lavishly for educational purposes; a vast educational system has been built up, residential and day schools have been established, hospitals have been built, and in times of stress, medical services provided for the sick and relief given the aged and destitute. For what purpose have these moneys been spent, especially those moneys spent so lavishly upon the education of the Indian, if not ultimately to bring him to the point where he may enjoy the full status of citizenship? In other words, these moneys have been spent to help take the Indian from a position of wardship, and place him where

he may enjoy the privileges and responsibilities of self sustaining and self respecting citizenship.
May I say that at times I believe there is a mistaken public opinion sentimentalizing over our Indians to the effect that they should be spared all healthy discipline. If it is considered that the Indian must be a permanent charge upon the public, then to a great extent our present efforts are a waste of time. Is all self reliance. to be drained out of the Indian? As I have stated, we have been generous with the Indian, and rightly so. Certainly he has been treated as a ward, except in cases where he has voluntarily applied for enfranchisement. But, I think, Mr. Chairman. that our efforts are justified only upon the belief that some day 'he will emerge from that state of dependence. I do not think that we are helping the Indian when we impress upon him the belief that he is never to be held responsible. Certain objections have been raised in committee based on the assumption that the department is going to enforce compulsory enfranchisement. That is not so, because if one reads the amendment carefully he will observe that the Indian is to be enfranchised only after his fitness for such enfranchisement has been passed upon by a board consisting of any judge of any superior court, or any judge of any circuit or county court, an officer of the department and a member of the band to which the Indian belongs. Such board shall make inquiry and report as to fitness. I believe that provision makes it perfectly clear that the Indian is not to be submitted to compulsory enfranchisement, but is to be enfranchised only after a proper investigation has been held.
At the present time an Indian may voluntarily apply for enfranchisement. Before that recommendation is passed on to His Excellency in council a most minute, exhaustive and careful investigation is held as to his fitness. To my mind, the officer or member of that board who will wish particularly to be assured beyond all peradventure as to the Indian's fitness for enfranchisement, will be the member representing the department. We do not enfranchise the Indians simply because they ask for it. We make an exhaustive analysis because we feel our responsibility in the matter, and we know that to enfranchise him before he is fit would not be in his interests, the interests of the government or anyone else concerned.
The hon. member for Brant (Mr. Smoke) speaking about compulsory enfranchisement, referred to the Six Nations Indians. He made further reference to the so-called Haldimand

Indian Act
treaty or agreement, and the Simcoe deed. I have those documents before me, but as he has read from them to the committee I do not think I would be serving any useful purpose by reading them again. May I say however that if -there is anything in any treaty or agreement which gives any Indians in Canada special privileges, it is amply provided for in the amendment now before the committee, which reads:
Provided that no enfranchisement of any Indian or Indians shall be made under this subsection in violation of the terms of any treaty that may have been entered into between the crown and the Indians of the band in question.
I have read several of these treaties to which reference was made by the hon. member for Brant, and I am unable to find that the amendment will effect any violation of the terms of any treaty or agreement made. But if there is any such violation, it is amply covered by the provisions of the amendment.

Whilst under the amendment the enfranchisement of an Indian may not appear to conflict with any treaty, would not the enfranchisement itself, in many cases, -conflict with what Indians regard as their treaty rights? For example would it not conflict with certain immunities they have, such as the right to hunt in and out of season, the right to draw treaty payments, the right to live on a reserve, and the right of freedom of property from seizure. Would any of these rights be interfered with by enfranchisement?

I should like to ask a question in line with that asked by the hon. member for Bow River. Is it the intention to enfranchise the Indian and allow him to remain a member of the band?
Mr. MURPHY': If the Indian became enfranchised certainly he would not any longer be a member of the band. I do not know whether the hon. member for Bow River has a copy of the amendment-
Yes, I have.

He will find that the amendment is as follows:

But we have on the other side the fact that when we took over the Indian holdings in Canada we bought them at extremely low valuations, and if we have spent money on the Indians since it is only what we ought to have done. That is not a sound position to take. Then we are told by the minister

Mr. MeINTOSH:	Then why take away

I would think that the end of education is to develop the capacity of the individual -to ask questions and answer them. That is the purpose of our training institutions, -to develop that power in the human mind. If we cannot do that we are not getting very far. If the Indian does not ask the question, and does not say, I want to be enfranchised, why enfranchise him? Apparently with all our culture and training we are afraid of the Indian not wanting to be enfranchised, and so want to impose it on him. To me that looks like enfranchising the Indian to get his vote. That should not be the end of any legislation; what should concern us is the welfare of the Indian.
Another matter I wish to mention is this. Does this committee think fair the stand we are taking against the Indian wearing his aboriginal costume? As I understand the law now, before he can take part in a dance or stampede or exhibition in his aboriginal -costume he must have permission from the agent or the department. Now we are wiping out that provision, and it would appear that we are t^ing to prohibit the Indian wearing his native costume anywhere, on the reserve or off -it. I cannot see why we are making a move of that kind. I believe the Indian is absolutely entitled to wear his Indian costume wherever he likes, and the disapproval of the department is simply intimidating the Indian and keeping him from developing in the continuity of freedom and liberty. We know what took place in Scottish history after the union of the parliaments in 1707. In the uprising of 1745 some small-bore politicians and public men of the period in England decided that they had better forbid the Highland clans to wear their costume-

If they report, as they can under this amendment, that the Indian is fit to be enfranchised, then he may be enfranchised no matter how much opposed he may be to it. I very much dislike at this stage of the session taking up the time of the house reading these protests, but I do feel that the matter touches so vitally the happiness, the future comfort, and the right of the Indians to obtain a livelihood as they have done in the past that I must protest as strongly as I can. To the

Sirs,-
On the report in the press that the government of the Dominion of Canada are in the consideration of enacting an act of parliament to force the Indians of the Dominion of Canada into compulsory enfranchisement, we, the members of the Chippewa-Thames Band of Indians of the . Caradoc agency, do herein make our humble protest to such enactment of the act of parliament for the following reasons:
The Indians of this part of the province of Ontario are not in a position of qualification to enter into such enfranchisement by education and temperament, and the fact that the smartest of our race living in the various reserves of the province of Ontario who have taken enfranchisement have in a few months, or years, lost all their property, and in most cases have had to receive help. The majority

of the Indians have not even a common or public school education, and therefore cannot compete with the white people.
The Indians from the earliest times have appreciated their treatment by the British crown. Their loyalty has been traditional. In 1876 and 1812 they gave valuable military assistance to our cause. Therefore, we, your petitioners, request your favourable consideration of this, our humble petition.
I wish to have this petition in the 'hands of 'the minister so that he may consider it. Powless, written to the Mail and Empire of Toronto. I will not trouble the committee by reading the whole of it but I would quote this part:

Apart from the question of good faith with the Indian, I do not think it can be denied that this is a breach of the relationship that has existed under the treaties that have been entered into at various times, even before the declaration of independence of tlhe United States, because I believe it was before that time that the main treaties were entered into, an undertaking having been given by the king in the old treaties that the Indians would be protected, that they would have their hunting grounds and fishing rights, to quote a saying so much used by the Indians themselves, "as long as grass grows and water runs." These rights were to be preserved; they could not have their property taken away from them if the white man got a judgment against them. That is the great, protection which is being taken away by these amendments to the act.

That comes from Frank Montom, a member of the Madfourth band. The Indian of two or three generations ago who lived among his own kind was better off than the Indian of today who is living partly with whites and partly with other Indians. There is no question at all that this is a breach of faith with the Indians. At this of all times, when there is so much unrest abroad in the land this should not be done. I shall not refer to the great possibilities in times of elections, but I repeat again that this is a breach of faith and the taking away of rights which these Indians have enjoyed for generations. Besides the Six Nations Indians, the Caughnawagas, the St. Regis Indians, the Muneeys and the Chippawas and the Blackfeet Indians have all sent me protests against this legislation. These Indians got along in the past without this legislation and there is no reason why it should be forced upon them at this time. 4.	Follow the Indian mode of life.
Evidently the persons to whom Mr. Nicholson refers do not fall within the first or second categories.
Mr. Williams informs me that the department does not know of any irregular band in the part of Canada referred to by Mr. Nicholson, so that evidently not one of them can fall within the first three categories, and those persons who live in the town in which Mr. Nicholson lives and to whom he refers specifically, evidently do not follow the Indian mode of life. These persons are, therefore, not Indians or non-treaty Indians within the meaning of the Indian Act and, so far as I am aware, have the rights of citizenship as other Canadians have and are entitled to the franchise.
The Deputy Superintendent General, Department of Indian Affairs,
Ottawa.

Can the minister now tell us the number of Indians who have been enfranchised on their own application? I understood him to say that none had been enfranchised on the application of their respective bands.

I said not to my knowledge. On a former occasion I.gave the information which the hon.- gentleman now asks for, but I can get it for him in a moment. But I wish to point out that here are Indians not following the mode of Indian life but who may have ninety-eight per cent of Indian blood in their veins, and who are to-day recognized as citizens of Canada with all the privileges and responsibilities of citizenship. Then we have other Indians in Montreal and Toronto and other large cities, members of the legal and medical professions, who beyond all doubt have received a much higher education and advanced much further than the class of Indians to which I have just referred, and yet who to-day are classed as Indians and have not the privilege of Canadian citizenship.
Is the minister willing to limit the legislation to those two classes of Indians?

I think the amendment as drafted amply covers the point in question. The board which will be appointed will certainly make full inquiry as to the fitness of the Indian. The hon. member for West Middlesex said that the Indian might not even be seen by the board and might not know anything about the matter until after the board

Indian Act
had made its report. But the act as it stands on the statute book to-day provides:
In the course of such inquiry it shall be the duty of the board to take into consideration and report upon the attitude of any such Indian towards his enfranchisement, which attitude shall be a factor in determining the question of fitness.
Certainly the board could not determine that question unless the Indian was before them; that is if it is going to do its duty, and I cannot conceive that they would do otherwise. May I again impress upon the committee this faot, that the member of the board who from my own personal knowledge will be very careful as to the recommendations will be the departmental representative. It is not necessary for me to go over the ground which has been so well covered by the Prime Minister so much better than I, but I did wish to answer those few objections.

Replying to the Prime
Minister's answer to my argument, I think the Prime Minister has not given this section the thought he usually gives to a section of an act which he endeavours to interpret. There can be no question whatever that this section puts the Indian in an entirely different category from what he ever was in before. That is what it is intended for. Why? Because as matters stand at the present time there have been no applications by the band. That is the best evidence as to whether the members of the band themselves think some of their number should be enfranchised. Secondly, because the applications made by the Indians themselves for enfranchisement have been very, very few. Perhaps the minister has the number now. At all events they are very few, a very small proportion, less than one one-hundredth of one per cent possibly. That is the best evidence as to the attitude of the Indian himself. If the Prime Minister's argument means anything, it means that by this bill we are not violating the right which the Indian now has to say that he shall not be enfranchised against his wish. That is the point I was making. I say that under this amendment the Indian may be enfranchised against his wish. That is what the amendment is aimed at. If you intend to consult him about it he can be enfranchised already under the provisions to which the Prime Minister referred. The Prime Minister argued that under section 110, which reads:
Upon the application of an Indian of any band-
That is, upon his application, or upon the application of the band-
-on a vote of a majority of the male members of such band-
There are two ways in which he may now be enfranchised. Under the bill as originally drawn, those were both cut out; the whole section was repealed. The bill as originally drawn prompted the amendment which was moved with a view partially to meet the objections made by the hon. members on this side of the house. As originally drawn the bill repealed subsection 1 of section 110, that which was read by the Prime Minister, and the following was substituted therefor:
The superintendent general may appoint a board to consist of two officers of the department and a member of the band to which the Indian or Indians under investigation belongs, to make inquiry and report as to the fitness of any Indian or Indians to be enfranchised.
That was the change.
Is the hon. member reading from the original act?

No; I have made it perfectly clear that I am reading the amendment. The bill as drawn provided, and the reason is very apparent, that because the Indians themselves did not make application to be enfranchised, or because the band did not make any, we must have some new system. The amendment provided for a board, as set out in the bill. It is true that a further amendment to section 110 has been moved, but that does not help the poor Indian who is being enfranchised against his will,-not one particle; it all amounts to the same thing.
An Indian who formerly could not be enfranchised without his consent or without the consent of the band to which he belonged can now, upon recommendation, be enfranchised by the board set up by the bill.
Some discussion has taken place as to what position the Indian would be in after enfranchisement. If the minister will look at subsection 9 of section 110 he will find exactly the position in which the Indian would be.
The superintendent general shall also pay to each Indian upon enfranchisement his or her share of the funds-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is the position they are in to-day.

I will say that is the position they would be in to-day if they were making application under subsection 1, which
Indian Act

they are not doing, and which this amendment seeks to change. Subsection 9 reads:
The superintendent general shall also pay to each Indian upon enfranchisement his or her share of the funds to the credit of the band, including such amount as the superintendent general determines to be his or her share of the value of the common interest of the band in the lands of the reserve or reserves, or share of the principal of the annuities of the band capitalized at five per centum, out of such moneys as are provided by parliament for the purpose or which may be otherwise available for such purpose.
Where does that leave your Indian? It leaves him with the money in his pocket, money which he cannot keep in his pocket or anywhere else. It makes him-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: He would be in the same position as he is to-day, if he were enfranchised.
But he is not being enfranchised to-day. Can the minister tell-
He does not want it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is for the country's sake.
During the ten year period from December 31, 1922, to December 31, 1932, under sections 122a of the old act and 114 of the new, 793 Indians were enfranchised.
How many under section 110?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Section 110 is in the old act.
Under section 110 of the old act 61 Indians were enfranchised during the same period.
Is that during a ten year period?
Yes, under section 110.

Sixty-one Indians were
enfranchised under one clause, and none under the other, in a ten year period.
Not much urge there.
Altogether there were 793.

And that is the position they are in now. There are some pieces of legislation which look worse, the more you examine them. This is one of the worst examples. Under those two clauses in ten years only 61 Indians received enfranchisement, or an average of six and one-tenth Indians per year. That figure is from a total of about
100,000	Indians. Hon. members will note that enfranchisement which may take place would 
be against the wish of the Indians. That is the situation. The more we examine and discuss the legislation, the worse it appears. It is absolutely useless for the Prime Minister or anybody else to attempt to argue that the Indian will be in anything like the position he was in before. His rights are being taken away from him. He will have money paid to him, and there is no hon. member in this committee who is not familiar enough with the Indian mind to know that money just slips through his fingers as quickly as it does through the fingers of some white people. To put into his hands cash representing the lands he formerly owned and of which he could not deprive himself is, in my view, an abandonment of a duty which for generations the government of Canada has observed. Assuming he gets one, two., three, four or even five thousand dollars for his rights, you may depend he will be on the road inside of a year. That is what will happen to him. His land and his money will be gone.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The time to say that was before the law was changed to permit enfranchisement at all.
No, no.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Anybody knows that. An argument such as the hon. member has made would be laughed at in any court of law.

It would be impossible to add much to what has been said by the hon.
. member for West Middlesex, but after reading the amendment I feel exactly as I did when I rose to answer the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Hear, hear.

Under the existing act the Indian must ask for enfranchisement. Under the amendment that privilege is left, but it is also the privilege of the superintendent general, if he wishes, to enfranchise Indians.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is not; why say that, when you know it is not so?
I have read the amendment.
The superintendent general may not do it.
Then the amendment of the minister simply provides that section 110 shall be left, and states further that the superintendent general may appoint a board-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is another matter.

Indian Act

Such board will report on the fitness of any Indian. And it shall have the same force and effect, and shall be dealt with in the same manner as if it had been made upon the application of the Indian himself.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

If that does not provide that the same procedure shall follow the action of the superintendent general as follows the application of the Indian himself, then I am afraid someone else will have to interpret the language of the section.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is not what you said. Of course it does.

I cannot argue anything else than that the change enfranchises the Indian through the superintendent general in the same way as he would have sought enfranchisement himself. I cannot add anything to what has been said by the hon. member for West Middlesex to clarify that point. I join with him however in protesting to the Minister of the Interior that so far as my experience in the province of Ontario has been, he would do well to accept the advice of the hon. member for West Middlesex.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Ten or twelve years ago was the time to give it.

Probably so. I agree
with the hon. member for Brant that the lands of these Indians so enfranchised will pass into the hands of white men who are not necessarily desirable on the reserve, and that the reserves will run down. I believe that some reserves in Ontario are improving greatly. The Indians have some splendid teachers, some splendid missionaries. The Cape Croker reserve I know sent practically every ablebodied man to the war. Those men are voting now. They are improving year by year under good guidance. I do not believe they are going to do as well if a number of whites are allowed to get possession of land now held by the Indians. For my part I agree with the hon. member for West Middlesex that the best evidence that the Indians do not want enfranchisement is the fact that they have not applied for it, and I think the minister will have to show us some other reasons why enfranchisement for which they do not ask should be forced upon them.

It may be presumption for a layman to enter into discussion with lawyers on matters of this kind, but the way the matter appears to me is simply this. There are now two methods whereby an Indian may
secure enfranchisement and this amendment proposes a third. If the amendment has any purpose whatever it must be that more Indians should be enfranchised. Evidently under the two methods now existent they are not being enfranchised in sufficient numbers and the object of the amendment is to increase the number. Whether deliberately or not, the Prime Minister only confuses the issue when he says that the results following enfranchisement by this new method will be just the same as those which follow to-day. Naturally they will, so why raise the point? The results will be the same no matter what method is employed. I say again that the purpose of this amendment is that more Indians should be enfranchised. Few are being enfranchised, on application by the individual himself, and none, I understand on application by the band. For some reason the department wants more Indians enfranchised so they propose this new method. I think the hon. member for West Middlesex and others have made it very clear that it is not desirable that any more Indians than at present should be placed in control of their property. That is how it appears to me, and the argument of the Prime Minister has absolutely failed to show me any reason why I should change my opinion.

I rise for only one purpose, to express the wish of the Indian bands in my riding, of which there are two, that they should be enfranchised. I think there must be a great diversity of intelligence among the Indians in the ridings of different members, or there would not be such diversity of opinion on this question in this house. The Indians in my riding are quite intelligent people, I would say their .intelligence is almost as high as that of the average white man. They have asked me time and again to try to get them enfranchised. I think they should be enfranchised w.herev.er they are intelligent enough. I think when an Indian has reached the stage of education and intelligence at which he is qualified to shoulder the responsibilities of citizenship they Should be given to him.

Will my hon. friend permit a question? Would he tell the committee how many applications came during the last ten years from Indians in his riding who are anxious to be enfranchised? I understand there were just sixty-two in the whole of Canada, so I wondered how many came from that riding.

I have not the figures,
I know there have been a certain number. I tell the committee this, that my trouble
Indian Act

has been to get them enfranchised. I have handled some applications myself, and have had to threaten the officials, not only of this government but other governments, that I would go over their heads to the minister to get them enfranchised, and I have done so. The present minister will bear me out in that statement. In my experience there seems to be a prejudice on the part of the officials against enfranchising these men. I think I told this committee on a former occasion of a man who came to me and protested that he could not get work on account of being a ward of the government. He had saved enough money to buy himself a large motor truck, and was as capable of earning a living as anyone else. Why shield these people after all? If they have the degree of intelligence and education to fit them for full citizenship why should they not have it?

They cannot wear their
full regalia!

That is the kind of
answer I would expect from the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot). Further, I would say that I think a great deal of the objection to this proposal comes from people who want to keep the privilege of being wards of the law. I think there is no doubt about that, they want to hide behind the law so they do not have to pay their debts. I say this parliament and this country have a duty to these people, and when they are ready for full citizenship but will not seek it we ought to make them take it. How are you going to develop responsible, self-respecting people unless you make them take the responsibilities of citizenship?
There are some things about the bill that I do not like or I am not clear about. I do not like the idea of allowing whites to mix with them and get their land, I think that is detrimental to the interests of this country, but I gather from the discussion that that is not a new thing. If it can be prevented I think it is desirable to do so, not only in the interests of the Indian but in the interest of that lower strata of white people who seem to want to mix with any inferior class. I would like to see that prevented if possible. But I would support the minister by telling him that the Indians in my riding have told me time and again that they want to be enfranchised and become full citizens of Canada.

I understand 62 Indians
were enfranchised by their own request?
There are different sections of the act which apply.
I mean under section 110.

During the ten year period from December 31, 1922, to December 31, 1932, under section 122a of the old act and section 114 of the new, that is the act now before us, 793 Indians were enfranchised. Under section 107 of the old and section 110 of the new act 61 were enfranchised during the same period. I may say that practically all Indians that are enfranchised to-day are enfranchised under section 114 rather than section 110.

What amount did these
various Indians receive out of the moneys of the band, under subsection 9 of section 110?
I have not that information at hand but doubtless I could get it.

I should be greatly obliged if the minister could give it because it has a very material bearing. We were wondering whether it would be one thousand, two thousand or five thousand that each would get, and I am advised that frequently it did not amount to even one thousand. When it is pointed out to the minister that this legislation is taking away the Indian's land and home and the protection afforded him, giving him one thousand dollars in cash, I think it will be apparent at once that the Indian will be on unemployment relief.

There are in my county
two Indian bands and I have never yet known of any Indian who applied for enfranchisement and was refused. The Indians on the reserve enjoy certain rights with respect to their land and property and I remember one attempt that was made in 1917 to expropriate the lands of the old Indians in Resti-gouche opposite Campbellton and to settle them in the northern country, the purpose being to take those lands as an annex to Campbellton and to set up building lots. That was prevented by the parliament of Canada. The Indians have been left on their reserves for their own protection, and I can recall that when a law was passed to enfranchise the Indians it was immediately repealed. Some Indians are competent to vote, and those who served overseas vote to-day in my constituency as in other parts of the country. But so far as Bonaventure is concerned I think it would be a great misfortune to enfranchise these Indians, leaving them to roam about away from the reserves, taking the little money they might get and spending it. It would merely add to the ranks of the unemployed, which are already numerous enough. I think the law should stand as it is now.	[DOT]

Indian Act
I asked a question with regard to the costumes of the Indians under the proposed legislation, and I wish the minister would be good enough to amplify his statement on that point.
That clause was considered by the committee and passed several weeks ago.

I am not asking what
was passed; I am asking the minister for a definite statement on the situation.

I do not wish to be discourteous to the hon. member, but if he would frame his question differently I might possibly be able to give him the information. He spoke some minutes ago but I am not clear as to what information he does want.

The proposed measure,
I understand, will interfere with the right of the Indian to wear his Indian costume off the reserve. Does this legislation further prohibit him doing so? Does it interfere with that aboriginal right? If it does, it is absolutely wrong.

That question was
thoroughly discussed in the house and if the hon. member was not present I can only regret the fact. But the section having been passed, I do not think we should be asked to rediscuss the matter now.

For some years I have been receiving an interesting illustrated catalogue advertising the so called stampede at Calgary. Would this legislation interfere with such an exhibition, where the Indians are allowed to roam in their Indian costumes?
That is the question I have asked and which, the minister refuses to answer. He says it has already been answered.

I think that the various suggestions that have been made might be embodied in an amendment as follows:
In respect of an Indian or Indians of any band who has not or have not made application for enfranchisement under this section or under section 114 of this act, the superintendent general may appoint a board to consist of any judge of any superior court or any judge of any circuit, district or county court, an officer of the department and a member of the band to be selected by the band to which the Indian or Indians under investigation belongs or belong, or failing the selection of such member for a period of thirty days after the date of notice having been given to the council, the member shall be appointed by the superintendent general-
That will be found in subsection 2 of section 110 now in respect of other questions of a similar character.
-to make inquiry and report as to the fitness of any Indian or Indians to be enfranchised, and such report shall have the same force and effect and shall be dealt with in the same manner as if the same had been made upon the application of an Indian or Indians under this section: Provided that no enfranchisement of any Indian or Indians shall be made under this subsection in violation of the terms of any treaty, agreement or undertaking that may have been entered into or made between or by the crown and the Indians of the band in question.
So far as the effect of this proposal is concerned, it merely recognizes the existing laws and protects the Indian against any possible undertaking that may have been given in any treaty or agreement, and the provision for selecting a member of the band is exactly what the law now is with respect to the case in which an Indian (makes his own application, namely, subsection 2 of section 110. I move that amendment.
Is this amendment to replace the one before the committee?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
Do I understand that the amendment we have been discussing is withdrawn?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: With the consent of the chamber, yes.

Would the minister consider adding to the amendment just offered something which I shall propose? I realize that a good deal of the time of the house is being taken up with this question, which to some hon. members may seem of no importance. I do not look upon it in that way at all; I think it is important, for it means everything to the people involved. With regard to the provision that no enfranchisement of any Indian or Indians shall be made under this subsection in violation of the terms of any treaty, I want to point out the difficulty of applying this, assuming that a case arose, as it would. An Indian comes and says, "This is in violation of a treaty". Unfortunately these treaties were made long before Canada had a government of its own. They were made in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Some of the first treaties were entered into in the seventeenth century, long before the declaration of independence, and involved the Indians who were in what is now the United States as well as those
Indian Act

then in what is now Canada, because it was then all British territory. It is very difficult to get hold of these old treaties. If I understood the minister correctly, he is unable to tell us at the present time, and I doubt whether any hon. member can tell us, what the treaty rights all are. I think there would be difficulty in establishing precisely what the treaty rights are under these old treaties of several hundred years ago. There is however one fact which he will not have much difficulty establishing and that is that for centuries under these treaties these rights have been recognized, including the right of protection given the ward of the government, not permitting him to alienate his property. I wonder if the Prime Minister and the minister would agree to the amendment reading like this:
No enfranchisement of any Indian or Indians shall bp made under this subsection in violation of the terms of any treaty, agreement or undertaking that may have been entered into or made between or by the crown and the Indians ot the band m question, or against the will of the Indian whom it is proposed to enfranchise.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
You cannot make it
negative.
Unless he is willing to consent, he should not be enfranchised.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. member overlooks the fact that for fifteen years the law has contained provisions for the enfranchisement of Indians.
Voluntary enfranchisement.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Not voluntary; by action of the band, if necessary. This committee will be made up of a member of the band, a representative of the superintendent general, and a judge of the superior or county courts. That is a precaution which does not exist with respect to the other two cases. Inasmuch as no such provision as that mentioned by the hon. member for West Middlesex has heretofore found its place in the law, the suggestion I have just made in the amendment with respect to treaties, agreements or undertakings made between or by the crown and the Indians would be ample to protect the interests of the Indian in the view of the judge who would have to be a member of the committee to determine the matter. The judge would be the impartial member, while there would be a member appointed by the government and one by the band. If the judge and the Indian say "no" there would be no doubt about the fact that there would 
be no enfranchisement. The answer to all the arguments which have been made this afternoon about the terrible white trash that is going to take away the people's land-
They cannot take the lands away from them.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: -the terrible white trash that might settle upon them, is the fact that the Indian's anxiety to secure money or land has not been evidenced by a desire to secure enfranchisement. I think it may be taken that the exercise of this power, provided it is done with caution and care, will not act unfairly in the determination of the fitness for enfranchisement. Tire judge of the county or superior court will be the impartial member on the committee. I think the amendment as it now stands makes the four principles much more fair.

The department has always to face the serious question as to whether or not certain individual Indians should be enfranchised. I found that there was opposition sometimes by the band itself against the desire of an individual Indian to be enfranchised. There was always difficulty in getting settlement with the band for his share of the fund and his interest in the lands. I think there must be the same difficulty in that regard as was stated by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario, because when I had the honour to preside over the department I found that there was a desire to allow Indians to become enfranchised. The logical outcome of Indian life is his merging into the life of Canadian citizenship, but it should not be forgotten that we allow individuals to come to Canada from all over the world without forcing enfranchisement upon them.
They are not wards.
Up to date we have not done so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
We put prohibitions
against them.

The chairman of this board which is to pass upon the fitness of an Indian to be enfranchised may be a judge, but the whole say as to whether or not final action shall be taken will be in the hands of the superintendent general. Under the present act he cannot do that unless the Indian is willing or an application is made by the band. Hon. gentlemen opposite are proposing something different from that at present in the act. As to the lands or prop-

Indian Act
erty owned by the band passing into the hands of white men, that cannot happen. The band takes good care of that. Before an individual becomes enfranchised they see that a settlement is made and an amount arrived at to represent his interest. That is given to him and the lands of the band are preserved. I do not think that principle should be interfered with. So far as the precautions set out in this subsection are concerned, they refer merely to the fitness of the individual Indian to be enfranchised. Whether or not he desires it, his case will be in the hands of the superintendent general. I doubt very much if this action will prove to be popular with the Indian. So far as securing votes are concerned, I think the superintendent general will be out of luck.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, quite so.
Do not impute motives.

Personally I think the government are making a mistake. I regret the slowness with which enfranchisement takes place and I know the difficulties of Indians having property and being on the highways and all that; it is rather a difficult situation, but I doubt the advisability of leaving the final say in the hands of the superintendent general. There is always the possibility of a favourable report by the board despite the protests of the individual or possibly of the band itself. If this is the case, the Indian will not be a very happy individual, and I do not think the Indians as a whole will consider that their interests are being protected.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: We will withdraw the original amendment which did not contain the necessary safeguard. Perhaps the chairman wrould read the last amendment.

The amendment reads:
That section 110 of the said act be amended by adding thereto the following subsection:
14. In respect of an Indian or Indians of any band who has not or have not made application for enfranchisement under this section or under section 114 of this act, the superintendent general may appoint a board to consist of any judge of any superior court or any judge of any circuit, district or county court, an officer of the department and a member of the band to be selected by the band to which the Indian or Indians under investigation belongs or belong, or failing the selection of such member for a period of thirty days after the date of notice having been given to the council, the member shall be appointed by the superintendent general to make inquiry and report as to the fitness of any Indian or Indians to be enfranchised, and such report shall have the same force and effect and shall be dealt with
in the same manner as if the same had been made upon the application of an Indian or Indians under this section: Provided that no enfranchisement of any Indian or Indians shall be made under this subsection in violation of the terms of any treaty, agreement or undertaking that may have been entered into or made between or by the crown and the Indians of the band in question.

As the amendment is pretty long and was not read sufficiently audibly for me, at least, to hear it, and much less to understand it, perhaps I may be excused if I do not discuss it at all and make my remarks refer to other phases of the matter. I suppose that will be quite in order, otherwise, we shall have to hear the amendment read again first.
There is one point on which I find myself in agreement with the minister and that is that some of the Indians, not now enfranchised, should be. I refer to the sons and daughters of Indian returned men who, by reason of their war service, were made eligible to vote. The returned men vote, but their sons and daughters do not. That matter would, I think, properly come under the election act and not under this. But lest some of my Indian constituents may have heard of the threatening redistribution bill hanging over their representative's head, and think, because of that, I may have lost all interest in my constituency, I believe I should say what I am about to say now. I am in favour of the sons and daughters of returned men having the same rights as have their fathers. Fancy, at this time when we are all trying to renounce war and we hear of the Kellogg-Briand pact and so on, enfranchising someone because he killed, or tried to kill, some fellowman in war! The son comes of age, becomes eventually a father himself and finds that neither he nor his wife can vote. His father has killed a man possibly; he is entitled to vote and he goes to the polls. The son says to himself: I have not killed or been given the opportunity of killing in war a man so I have not the franchise; I cannot vote. Whom shall I kill? He will look around and his keen hunter's eyes may light upon the Minister of National Revenue.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Upon the member for
the riding.

Nobody knows upon whose person the lynx-like eye of this Indian who cannot vote, may light. Whom shall he
select to massacre?

The hon. member seems to indicate whom he will select.
Indian Act
I have to take one of them and I have taken the one who seems to be the better prepared to pass away.
Oh, oh.

This matter is no joke, although we may for the moment make a joke about it. That is the actual condition on the reserve under the federal government. I have never discovered the solution to the knotty problem, but when one of these Indian boys came to my place and stayed there till twelve o'clock midnight explaining why his son should be enfranchised; that he was a good citizen; that he had taken up the peaceful occupation of pastoral as well as tillage farming and yet he could not vote, I had no answer and nobody has any answer to this complaint. If that situation could be corrected in the election act I would hold up both hands for it. I do not want to cause any more annoyance to the government than I can help; that is the spirit in which I make these comments. I know the Prime Minister does not care a snap of his finger about precedents; he is not governed by the hoary precedents of other countries, and he is right; in these days you have to break new ground. But I would like to know whether any other country under the sun ever forced its natives into enfranchisement. The whole history of native populations from time immemorial to the present day is that they have wanted the franchise before their mandatory government was ready to give it to them. This government is going to form the extraordinary precedent of compelling the natives of our country to become enfranchised with all that goes with that. The hon. member for West Edmonton pointed out that we do not do that to white people. So far as I know there are people who have lived from manhood up and died in Canada without taking out their naturalization papers. Why should we take, above all others, the sons and fathers of our own' natives, and compel them to become enfranchised?-because that is what the government is doing, describe it how they like. It is putting into the hands of this board the power to enfranchise these people. What is the only argument that I have heard in favour of taking this extraordinary step? I am speaking earnestly and sincerely because I know the Indian population of my constituency; I have known many of them since childhood, since they were in the cradle, and have seen them grow up and become useful citizens, following mainly agriculture. The band in my constituency is an excellent one-I do not mean the Six Nations-it is a musical band; they are accomplished in much that we call the

culture of the white people, and these Indians are superior to some whites. Why then Should we treat them any differently from the way we are using white immigrants in the way of voluntary enfranchisement?
The argument was that they had become so qualified in certain of the professions, I think it was law and medicine; that they had become too keen competitors for their white brothers. If that is so, it is not a great tribute to the work of the Indian department during the past decade, that these people should have been taken from the primitive condition in which we found them, roaming over the prairies, and been placed in our schools, eventually in our universities, so that now they have become so accomplished that they make the white men scratch gravel to compete with them? If so, let us continue that course of education further before we compel them to become citizens. If the argument advanced by the government is valid, I have not heard of any cases. I do not know in my experience of a single Indian who has gone into any of the professions and embarrassed the white man by his competition. There may be such cases, but the general policy of the department has been rather the other way. Life on the farm seems to be natural to the normal outdoor life of the Indian and he was discouraged from going into the professions for that reason and also because, if he did so, he had to meet some white man's prejudice against an Indian. Consequently this helped to cripple his activities in his competition with the white man. But if he is such an outstanding Indian that he can overcome the prejudice that some people of other colours than his hold against him, this is a great tribute to him and surely because of his attainments in this respect he should not be penalized by being enfranchised against his will. I think the government is making a terrible mistake and being unfair to itself. There is only one explanation of its conduct; though I do not like to suggest motives, there is only one conclusion-

The hon. member is
coming to it.

Yes, and I am going to get there yet. The conclusion is that this government is going to follow the example of the government that preceded the election of 1896, that I remember so well, in the heinous enfranchising acts they had that enabled the returning officers and scrutineers to do everything almost but hang an elector. While we have got away from that by thirty or thirty-five years, my thoughts go back to that time and in the absence of any other

Indian Act
objection or purpose I am driven to the conclusion that this government, by means of this law, will be enabled to go out before an election and convert Indians into voters wholesale. If not, let them put up some valid reason why they are passing this act. I have not heard any so far. I do not think you can quote a precedent on top of this earth where native people have been compelled to be enfranchised. I have had several conversations with the minister, some of them jocular and some serious, and he knows that I entertain this pretty well grounded suspicion, but if he insists upon putting this through I do not think we will waste an awful lot more time trying to prevent him. This is the fifth time this bill has been up before the committee. I spoke on three of the other occasions, and when this order was called this afternoon I went out. I had business of a most pressing nature with a party who wanted to see me, but when I came back into the chamber I found that we were at the exact section that we were discussing two months ago. It is true that there have been some changes. I have been moved for the reasons I have indicated to make these few observations, and when the time comes to amend the elections act I shall be delighted as I have already intimated, to support my hon. friend the minister or whoever has charge of it in giving the franchise to the sons and daughters of the returned men, even if they have not killed or tried to kill anybody in war.

I realize that the discussion has taken longer than I fancy most members of the committee anticipated. I have listened with a good deal of attention to what the Prime Minister said with regard to the amendment that he proposed. It does make a change in that the third member of the board shall be selected by the band, but it still leaves it in the position that that member is all right if the judge is with him, and he is all wrong if the judge and the other member of the board are against him. If he is seeking to protect the representatives of the band I wonder if the Prime Minister would not agree to putting in a provision that no resolution would carry unless it was supported by the vote of the representative of the band? But I do not suppose there is any use in advocating that. I want, however, to move an amendment that there shall be added to the section as proposed to be amended, the following words:
or against the will of the Indian whom it is proposed to enfranchise.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That would be out of
order, Mr. Chairman. It would negative the proposal.

We are amending subsection 110 by adding a subsection and what I have proposed is not a negative of anything in the proposed subsection. I wonder if the minister could now give us an idea of the amounts paid to the Indians.

I have not been able to
obtain it up to the present.
It will be given before the third reading of the bill?

I shall endeavour to get
the information for the hon. member. I want to deal with one point which was raised by the hon. member for Melville with reference to the enfranchisement of the Indians on the eve of an election. He indicated, as he did on a former occasion, that there might be some ulterior motive in the mind of the minister or of the department in proposing this amendment; in this case I suppose it would be the minister. May I say that his position is very illogical because if the Indian is to be enfranchised against his will, as hon. members to your left, Mr. Chairman, suggest, certainly he will not vote for the government that puts such voting power in his hands. Secondly, it cannot be done in that manner because subsection 5 of section 110 already provides:
On the report of the superintendent general that any Indian, male or female, over the age of twenty-one years, is fit for enfranchisement, the governor in council may by order direct that such Indian shall be and become enfranchised at the expiration of two years from the date of such order or earlier if requested by such Indian.
And so forth. That disposes completely of the point raised by the hon. member for Melville, that some government might enfranchise a number of Indians on the eve of an election. It simply cannot be done.

The section which the
minister has just quoted has a very much fuller meaning than he has given to it. It says:
On the report of the superintendent general that any Indian, male or female, over the age of twenty-one years, is fit for enfranchisement, the governor in council may by order direct that such Indian shall be and become enfranchised at the expiration of two years from the date of such order or earlier if requested by such Indian.
Those last few words just knock out the two-years argument altogether. Enfranchisement may be granted at once if the Indian asks for it.
Indian Act

The
question is on the subamendment.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That cannot be in order, Mr. Chairman. You cannot move an amendment that is a negative to an existing proposal. By voting against it hon. members vote in favour of the amendment.

How many people
with both their lugs all right have heard that and understand what it is?
We heard it.

All right. I do
not know if my hon. friend from Pictou heard it with his auricular appendage on, but I did not. If I was right on top of it I could not understand it. It is not fair to the committee. We do not know what they are agreeing to. Will someone interpret the amendment in language we can understand, not draftsman's language, but every day language?
Does the hon. member say he does not understand the subamendment moved by the hon. member for West Middlesex?
Let it go.

I consider that the subamendment moved by the hon. member for West Middlesex simply repeats section 110 of the act. I am opposed to the amendment which was submitted by the minister on the ground that section 110 does provide for enfranchisement at the instance of the individual or of the band. The amendment moved by the minister simply provides that the superintendent general may initiate the inquiry to determine whether the Indian shall be enfranchised. I am opposed to the amendment on the ground that the Indians do not want enfranchisement as is evidenced by the fact that they have not applied for it under the original section as it now stands. I also submit that the minister misrepresented subsection 5 of section 110 when he pointed out to the hon. member for Melville that even if an Indian were enfranchised before the election he would have to wait for two years. Either deliberately or innocently the minister left out a few. words in the subsection which point out that if the Indian so desires, such enfranchisement may take place at once. So the minister's answer to the hon. member for Melville is not an answer at all. I think the committee might just as well vote. We are opposed to the amendment as offered by the minister and we may as well record ourselves as being so opposed.

I am glad I did
not hear it.
