speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed from Friday, February 17, consideration in committee of Bill No. 26, to amend the Exchequer Court Act-Mr. Guthrie.-Mr. Cowan (Port Arthur) in the chair.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
This bill was discussed last
on February 17. As pointed, out at that time [by my colleague the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie), it is a well known principle of British law that moneys paid in settlement of a claim or of a litigated matter, when there has been no fraud or threat of any kind made, cannot be recovered. It is further a principle of British law, as my colleague pointed out, that money paid in mistake of law cannot be recovered. The Minister of Justice added that the object of the amendment is to declare that in Canada, in actions or proceedings taken before the exchequer court, the common principle of British law shall apply, and that the law in that respect shall be general throughout the length and breadth of Canada. The effect would be that in all matters coming within the jurisdiction of the exchequer court no party would be able to set up a claim to the effect that he should get his money back because he had paid it under a mistake of law.
Last February the hon. member for Mont-magny and the ex-Minister of Justice expressed some doubts as to whether or not there would be some encroachment upon the rights of the province of Quebec. They expressed the opinion that Bill No. 26 relates to property and civil rights in the province of Quebec and for that reason might be ultra-vires, in so far as it might come into conflict with property and civil rights of that province. On the other hand my colleague the Minister of Justice stated that in his opinion the amendment did not in any way come into conflict with the laws of the province of Quebec. There are provisions in the Quebec code through which moneys can be recovered when paid in mistake of law, and no one for a moment proposes to disturb that provision. But the exchequer court is a federal court having jurisdiction in all parts of Canada. The Minister of Justice added that it is not in-

Exchequer Court Act
tended in any way to disturb the operation of the law of the province of Quebec, as it applies to residents of that province, or to any matter which arises in that province. However the discussion on the bill was adjourned in order to allow the hon. member for Quebec East to express his views. The committee would be pleased at this time to hear from him.

I am very happy indeed that the government agreed not to proceed with the bill upon the first occasion. At that time I had doubts which have since changed into a certainty. This bill would do indirectly what parliament cannot do directly. Its true title ought to be: An Act to Supersede the Civil Code of the Province of Quebec. I believe I will have no difficulty in demonstrating that assertion. As is shown in the explanatory note, section 18 of the Exchequer Court Act gives exclusive jurisdiction to the exchequer court in respect of any matter which might be the subject of a suit or action against the crown, and so on.
Section 5 of the Petition of Right Act, which is chapter 168 of the revised statutes of Canada, enacts that all petitions of right must come before the Exchequer Court of Canada.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: That is the procedure.

Yes. The Minister of Justice claimed that the bill would not take away any rights enjoyed by citizens of the province of Quebec. Well, it does not take the rights away; they will have the rights, just the same, but they will have no tribunal before which they may appear, because the exchequer court is the only one before which their rights could be presented. A petition of right must come before the exchequer court; by this bill the exchequer court will be deprived of jurisdiction in the matter of claiming amounts which have been paid to the crown in mistake of law. The purpose of the bill is pretty clearly stated, although it is not said that it is for the purpose of preventing the provisions of the civil code of the province of Quebec from operating. It is said in the explanatory note that the object of the bill is to effect uniformity of the law throughout Canada in regard to the recovery of any money paid to His Majesty voluntarily in mistake of law. My hon. friend has been honest and sincere; he says it is a principle of British law that there is no recovery of moneys that have been paid in mistake of law, and he wants this British principle to 53719-297
apply everywhere. Well, I know it is the law in all the provinces which are under the common law, but it is not the law in the province of Qeuebec.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: You mean on account of articles 1047 and 1140?

Of articles 1047 and 1140 of the civil code, which I am going to read:
1047. He who receives through error of law or of fact what is not due him is hound to restore it; or if it cannot be restored in kind, to give the value of it.
If the person receiving be in good faith, he is not obliged to restore the profits of the thing received.
1140. Every payment presupposes a debt; what has been paid where there is no debt may be recovered.
There can be no recovery of what has been paid in voluntary discharge of a natural obligation.
I do not want to discuss the advantage or disadvantage of the law, whether the provisions of the civil code are better, more equitable, than those of the common law. I personally believe that when through a mistake in law a man has paid money which is not due there is much in favour of the law that says he has the right to claim it back. It is not the law elsewhere but it is in the province of Quebec. It is the French law; it is a matter of property and civil rights. A man in the province of Quebec who in mistake of law has paid an amount which he does not owe has a civil right to claim it back, and parliament cannot take that right away from him. Parliament oamnot take it away from him directly, and parliament should not take it away from him indirectly by depriving him of the only tribunal before which he can lay -his claim.
. Section 94 of the British North America Act is very interesting in the discussion of this matter, because according to the explanatory note this bill is for the purpose of making the law uniform in all the provinces of Canada. Section 94, which deals with uniformity of laws, says:
Notwithstanding anything in this act, the parliament of Canada may make provision for the uniformity of all or any of the laws relative to property and civil rights in Ontario, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick, and of the procedure of all or any of the courts in those three provinces, and from and after the passing of any act in that behalf the power of the parliament of Canada to make laws in relation to any matter comprised in any such act shall, notwithstanding anything in this act, be unrestricted; but any act of the parliament of Canada making provision for such uniformity shall not have effect in any province unless and until it is adopted and enacted as law by the legislature thereof.

Exchequer Court Act

But this section does not apply to the province of Quebec. Parliament has the constitutional right to enact measures for the uniformity of laws in Ontario, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, and certainly in the other provinces which have since entered the confederation, and are under the common law; but even then such measures enacted by this parliament would have to be ratified by the provinces concerned. The province of Quebec is excluded from the operation of this section.
Section 101 of the British North America Act gives to this parliament the right to create federal courts. This section does not give to parliament the right to change the laws; it gives it the right to apply the laws. I submit that parliament has not the right indirectly to use the Exchequer Court Act, which creates this federal tribunal, for the purpose of taking away a civil right from any citizen of any province, as would be done if this bill becomes law; because, although as I say the right would still exist under the civil code, there would be no tribunal before which claims could be made; for petitions of right cannot now be tried by the superior court of the province as they were before the Exchequer Court Act was enacted. There has been no change of the law, but there has been a change of the locus. It is the tribunal that has been changed. This amendment would, I submit, take away the jurisdiction in the province of Quebec in matters of recovery of money paid in mistake of law. While the claim under the law would still exist, there would be no court where it might be entertained. So as I said at the opening of my remarks, parliament would do indirectly what it cannot do directly, namely interfere with the law of the province of Quebec in matters pertaining to property and civil rights.
Now the civil law, "repetition de l'indu," recovery of moneys paid in mistake, applied as well against the crown as against ordinary persons. I do not believe anybody can contradict that, and it has been well recognized by the house.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: That is the case of the Exchange Bank vs. the Queen?

Yes, it was decided in that case, and in a case of rather recent date, Ross vs. the King, the supreme court was unanimous to the effect that as the duties were paid at the port of Montreal the case was to be determined by the laws of the province of Quebec. And quite recently in the case of the King vs. Cutting, 1932 S. C.R., 410, the petition of right was maintained for the recovery of $13,513 paid to the province of Quebec for succession duties in mistake of law.
That was against the crown in the right of the province; it was not disputed.

But I believe the principle is the same. The crown in the right of the dominion is subject to the laws of the province of Quebec in matters pertaining to citizens of the province.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

I will conclude my remarks in a very few words. I have submitted and, I think, fairly shown that it is the right of a citizen of the province of Quebec who has paid money under a mistake of law to recover such money. This is a civil right which cannot be taken away by this parliament. Indeed, this bill shows that that is the opinion entertained even by its authors, because it is not being done in a direct way; they are not taking the right away from the citizen but the tribunal, the forum, the locus where he could state the claim to recover that money.
The other objectionable feature of the bill to which I direct attention is its retroactive aspect. The bill reads, "to entertain any action heretofore or hereafter commenced." As a matter of fact, there are actual petitions of right, or at least requests for petitions of right pending against the crown, and even in respect of which fiats have been granted. If this bill becomes law it will be confiscatory, and I think it would be equivalent to expropriation without compensation.
I wish to read to the committee a resolution unanimously adopted by the council of the bar of Montreal, protesting against the bill. I will read it in French, as it has been sent to me:
(Translation)
Whereas Bill No. 26:	"to amend the
Exchequer Court Act" constitutes an infringement on the civil laws of the province of Quebec, in that it tends to render inoperative the provisions of the Civil Code in respect to recovery of moneys paid in error.
Whereas this bill might affect cases that are pending and that in principle all legislation infringing on acquired rights is contrary to equity and public order;
Therefore, the Council of the Bar, Montreal section, deem it their duty to protest against said bill and respectfully pray the Hon. Hugh Guthrie, Minister of Justice, not to proceed further in this respect
Unanimously.

Exchequer Court Act
I will read also a letter I have received from the assistant attorney general of the province of Quebec:
(Translation)
Quebec, February 24, 1933. Hon. Ernest Lapointe, K.C., M.P.,
56 St. Peter Street,
Quebec.
Dear Sir,-
Your letter of February 20th instant, relating to the amendments of the Exchequer Court Act, and addressed to the Hon. Prime Minister, was handed to me in order that I might examine the question to which it gives rise.
We are of the opinion that this act, after the amendment proposed by Bill No. 26, inasmuch els it affects persons resident in the province of Quebec, would in this respect constitute an infringement on the legislative powers of the province of Quebec as provided by subsection 13 (Property and Civil Rights in the Province) of article 92 of the British North America Act, 1867.
I am,	,
Yours sincerely,
The Deputy Attorney-General.
Under the circumstances, I think the committee will see that it is no whim on my part but that the stand I am taking against this bill is supported and indeed set forth by the bar of Montreal and by the provincial authorities of Quebec.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That there is an arguable question at issue in this case goes without saying. The civil law of the province of Quebec does provide that money paid under a mistake of law may be recovered equally as though it were paid under a mistake of fact. That is not the law in the other provinces, nor is it the law in England, although the Lord Chancellor, delivering judgment in a case in England, Cooper v. Phipps, many years ago said that under some circumstances a mistake of law might be a question of fact. However, that issue does not arise in this case.
That the civil rights of the citizens of Quebec are not to be in any sense restricted or taken away from them by legislation of this parliament is perfectly clear; they are guaranteed by the constitution and will be maintained by this parliament. As to that I think there is no question. The only issue is this. Is it competent for this parliament to enact legislation that will secure uniformity of treatment with respect to actions brought for recovery of money paid the crown under mistake of law? Undoubtedly the action could not be maintained in Ontario by an Ontario company, but the same company maintaining an office in Montreal and making payment there might, if the civil code is to be applied, recover the money.
Is that the general purpose of a federal court? I think not. I think the federal court 53719-297 J
idea, namely, the idea behind the exchequer court, was that all actions brought against the crown, of whatever character, should have general legal principles applied to them with respect to the statute of limitations and with respect to matters of that kind, unless there were a provision to the contrary in express terms. In this case the reason, for instance, that 'the retroactive feature is found in the act, is a simple one. The persons who are concerned have received the money; they have charged the money against their customers, and the subsequent decision of the courts would indicate that the principle on which the crown claimed from them was wrong. But they having claimed it from their customers and being unable to give it back, the individuals through whom it was recovered should not be able now to recover it and pocket that much more profit. That is a short way of putting it. If parliament adopted retroactive legislation under these circumstances, it would be pursuing the course pursued in Quebec itself with respect to election contests in provincial elections.
I have two suggestions to make to the hon. gentleman. I understand that the Minister of Justice and he discussed the matter, and I gather that he was of the opinion that it would not be proceeded with. If he was of that opinion we will respect his views in that regard. On the other hand, I suggest to him that this matter must ultimately be determined by the courts and we might enact this legislation, adding to it a section to provide that it should not come into force except on proclamation, with the understanding that in the meantime the statute would be referred to the supreme court for the purpose of having its validity determined. I leave either alternative to my hon. friend, but it does occur to me, in view of the questions that are at issue and must ultimately be settled-and the hon. gentleman has placed them before the committee in a most reasonable and fair way -that it might be desirable that we should pass the legislation, providing, as I have said, that it Should not come into force except on proclamation and after it had been referred, under the provisions of the Supreme Court Act, to that court for determination. That I suggest would meet the situation. In view of the discussions which the hon. gentleman had with the Minister of Justice, however, I repeat, if that course does not commend itself to him we will discharge the order for the moment.

I am grateful to my
right hon. friend for his suggestion, but I should prefer the first alternative, because I should not like to seem to agree to the prin-
Exchequer Court Act

ciple underlying the bill, even if we have to submit it afterwards to the Supreme Court of Canada. I suggest to my right hon. friend that he let this bill sleep for another year. In the meantime he might confer with the provincial authorities and next year if the government think they should proceed with it, it could be again presented. In the meantime I think it would be better to let the bill stand.

Does this bill apply to any province other than Quebec, and does it place any limitation upon the rights of the citizens in provinces other than Quebec to proceed before the exchequer court for the return of money paid in mistake of law?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I understand it applies to
all provinces, but if we agree to the views expressed by the hon. member for Quebec East, it would apply only to the provinces other than Quebec. This would be so because of the civil rights guaranteed to the citizens of that province by the British North America Act.

I do not pretend to
have anything but a very superficial knowledge of the situation, but as I understand it, the citizens of the province of Quebec have the constitutional right of proceeding against the crown for the recovery of money paid in mistake of law. Apparently this bill would nullify that constitutional right.
As far as the provinces other than Quebec are concerned, the law will remain as it is.

That is why I was
wondering if this bill would limit the rights enjoyed at the present time by provinces other than Quebec.

They have no such
right at the present time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The English law does
not permit one who has paid any money under a mistaken idea as to what the law is to recover that money. Let us take the gallonage tax as an example. Suppose I pay money under this tax and it turns out subsequently that my appreciation of the law is erroneous. In the eight provinces other than Quebec that money could not be recovered by an action in the exchequer court. If I paid $10 when the correct computation was $4, that could be recovered because that payment was made in mistake of fact. I am giving a simple illustration without going into technicalities, and I think the distinction between a mistake of fact and a mistake of law is illustrated by what I have just said.

In the province of Quebec, under the civil law, the question of the recovery of money paid in mistake of law is in exactly the same position as though it were paid in mistake of fact. In either case the litigant can bring his action. As the former Minister of Justice has pointed out, the effect of this legislation would be that no money could be recovered in any part of Canada, if paid in mistake of law. There would be a universal rule applied to all provinces. The question as to whether this is a matter dealing with substantive law under the authority given by the British North America Act to set up a federal exchequer court or a matter dealing with property and civil rights and remedies that are appropriate for the purpose of enforcing claims in connection with property and civil rights is disputable and arguable. I think that these matters could be settled by the courts in the manner I have indicated but I appreciate the point raised by the former Minister of Justice. If he has relied upon the conversations he had with the Minister of Justice to the effect that the issue was of such a doubtful character, this matter had better stand for further consideration. The Solicitor General will not press the bill for the Minister of Justice in his absence, and he can move that the committee rise.
As I understand it, at the present time the exchequer court has the right to hear such cases only when they come from Quebec?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I move that the committee rise.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
The house resumed from Friday, February 17, consideration in committee of Bill No. 30, to amend the Customs Act-Mr. Ryckman-Mr. Stirling in the chair.
On section 2-Special permission for lightening vessels and unlading goods.

I should like to reiterate the objection I made against this section when the bill was last before the committee. I do not think there should be an exception made for the lightening and unloading of vessels on Sundays. The explanatory note reads:
By permitting lightening and unloading on holidays and Sundays and after and before hours, heavy demurrage loss, amounting in many cases to $2,500 per day, can be avoided.

Customs Act
This explanation does not seem to justify the change being made in the laws of the country. I think this amendment comes in conflict with the Lord's day act, and I urge the minister to withdraw this particular part of the bill.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I move that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It seems to me, in any
event, the committee might amend it in this way, that if the vessel is unloaded on a Sunday, no action shall be instituted except by the attorney general of a province and no attorney of a province is apt to do so under the circumstances.
This is already provided under the Lord's Day Act.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
Section 3 agreed to.
On section 4-Prohibited or smuggled or unmanifested goods found in any vessel.

I would like to point out
what this section really means. The ostensible purpose of the amendment is to make the master liable to a penalty not exceeding $200 in one case and not exceeding $1,000 in another. That may or may not be justified in order to give the master a very particular interest in checking smuggling on his boat. But what I wish to draw attention to is the unjust provision in the part that is not being amended. The part that was there before states that if any prohibited or smuggled goods, or goods not in the manifest, are discovered on board the vessel, the whole boat with its sails, rigging, tackle, is liable to be seized and forfeited, with apparently no trial at all. Perhaps people think in terms of a little gas boat smuggling something, but supposing this were a big liner worth $300,000 or perhaps $400,000, and one of the crew smuggled some dope, and you can smuggle enough dope in the heel of your boot to give you a living for a year; or suppose a packet of cigarettes or a prohibited magazine were smuggled. In such a trivial case as that, in the discretion of the customs official the whole boat may be seized and forfeited. I do not think that is reasonable. We insert these provisions rather glibly or casually, more or less on the understanding that they wifi not be enforced, and certainly they should not
Customs Act

be, but why put them in? Is such a proceeding fair and just, supposing a member of the crew has committed a .petty infraction of the law? Let us suppose these boats carry Chinamen; in every trip of a boat there are new placed devised to smuggle dope which goes into small bulk; you can put enough heroin into a fountain pen to make it profitable, and because one of the crew does such a thing, the whole boat may be seized and forfeited What would the Canadian Pacific ocean services say if one of the Empress boats were seized and forfeited for such a reason?-and so far as I can see this can be done without even summary conviction. I would like the minister, if he can, to explain such an extraordinary provision.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
I would just like to say to the committee that this clause is in the spirit of the Customs Act. If my hon. friend will permit me, I hardly think he was fair in limiting the charge to the master of the vessel. What appears is that:
The master or person in charge of such vessel and any other person concerned in such breach or violation, shall be liable-
And so forth. In the case of a Canadian Pacific liner or any other craft, however large or small it may be, the person liable would be the one who was responsible. As my hon. friend knows, if a vehicle or a vessel, because vehicles and vessels of all kinds are covered in the Customs Act, is found carrying what I will call contraband of the act, it is forfeited, but what always happens is this, that the customs official ascertains who is to blame; the one who is to blame is proceeded against and the vehicle or the vessel is released. This penalty clause which appears in section 4 appears in six other sections of the Customs Act. I may tell the hon. gentleman I know of no case in which one who has been innocent has been saddled with the loss of his conveyance, be it vessel or vehicle, and I would not expect, if a clause such as this were put into the act, there would be taken by the Department of National Revenue any action which would be unfair to a man who was not guilty.

The argument in reply to my remarks was exactly as one would anticipate: First, that it was in the act before. I anticipated that and said that that did not make it any better. Secondly, the minister says that it occurs in six other sections. That certainly does not make it any better. If I had murdered a man, it would not be my defence that I had murdered six other men. Next the minister goes to the very opposite extreme and says that this is never used. That is what I was contending; if it is never used, 
why put it in? And if it should not be put in, why not eliminate it? Finally, the minister says that the procedure will be that they will seize the boat and ascertain the guilty party and release the ship. It is nothing to me whether they seize a Canadian Pacific boat or not; but would the minister tell me, and I ask in all seriousness, having once legally seized and forfeited the boat, apparently without trial, where he gets power to release it? He has no such power. He is going to seize the boat under this desperately arbitrary power, which he says is never enforced; but where does he get authority, once the boat is seized, to give it back?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The governor in council may do that. The first case of this kind that I recall was when, as a youth, I stepped into the court house in the little village in which I was born. A member of a crew had landed from a ship some goods which technically constituted smuggling. A collector of customs had seized the vessel and an action had been brought against the collector of customs. I well recall the counsel in that case, afterwards Mr. Justice Hannington. The plaintiff was non-suited, for the first time in his life, he said. This legislation is intended to operate as a deterrent and to prevent looseness in connection with the inspection of crews' quarters by the master and officers of the ship, so that narcotics will not be stored and taken ashore, as they might easily be if the severity of the penalty did not in itself ensure the strictest supervision by those chargeable with the responsibility.
Would not personal liability to a fine of SI,000 be sufficient?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, the master is
responsible for his ship. A provision of that character has long been in the British law, not that that makes it good, but it has been found that a deterrent of this character is the only deterrent that will ensure the master and officers of the ship searching and inspecting and taking every step to guarantee against the use of the vessel to which a member of the crew is articled for the purpose of promoting an illegal practice, the landing of goods that constitute smuggling. In practice it has been found a salutary deterrent, and in my judgment it should be extended.
While this is a severe punishment for the guilty party, would it not also be severe for the innocent owners of the vessel?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There has never been any complaint. If the innocence of the owners is established an order in council is always issued releasing the ship.

Soldier Settlement Act

It seems to me that this
section would apply not only to the crew but to the passengers on the vessel who were found with contraband, and the vessel would then be subject to seizure whatever might be the intent of the act. In the administration it works out something like this. I have had no experience with vessels other than prairie schooners, but when anybody in an automobile is found with contraband the car is seized and remains under seizure until the case is settled, generally several months after. If 37ou seize a ship and hold it for several months before releasing it, that would entail a tremendous loss to the owners. No matter what may be the intent of the act some customs officers are very strict and live up to the letter of the law, conceiving it to be their duty to find every possible means of getting convictions. They always take advantage of a strict interpretation of the act to make a seizure wherever possible, and in this case hardships would be worked. I do not give all customs officers throughout the country credit for having more than average intelligence, but it is a fact that some of them seem intent on getting convictions, just like some policemen, and very frequently cars and boats will be seized which in the end have to be released, but in the meantime very great inconvenience is caused to the owners.

I had a
case brought to my attention recently, which I turned over to the department. A man, was coming back across the boundary with his wife who had received some presents to the amount of less than five dollars in one of the American cities. They passed the customs officer but were detained by the Royal Northwest Mounted Police. The car was searched and seized. Before it was released they had to pay $18.60, which they have never recovered. That seems to me to be carrying things entirely too far.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
This relates only to
carriage by sea.

I quite appreciate that fact, but I am pointing out that the same hardship applies in the seizure of automobiles, only to a greater extent. They are not likely to seize a large vessel because one of the crew is found trying to smuggle, but a car is often seized and is tied up at once. I think the penalty is too severe for the small amount involved in such oases, and I think the penalty in this case is also too severe.

I would suggest that the
captain be sentenced to death. That would be a still greater deterrent. He could afterwards be revived and released.

When this bill first came up I intended to make a few remarks regarding the situation in British Columbia, but not wishing to delay the bill then I thought I would reserve what I had to say until the matter was in committee. I wish now to direct the attention of the minister to the condition of the settlers in British Columbia. I have here a brief issued by the soldier settlers' organization in British Columbia, and while I do not intend to read
Surely my hon. friend does not think that British Columbia is an exception in that regard.

I am sorry to say it is not an exception. It is stated that pictures, books and pamphlets were distributed in the camps overseas and these men were even asked where they would like to locate to take up this choice land. They were told they would become independent and the most glowing future was held out to them. They were almost compelled to take up this land. They claim the scheme was actually forced upon them. I know from personal contact with some of these settlers in British Columbia that many of them even assigned or commuted their pension as payment. However,

Soldier Settlement Act
in many cases dire necessity has forced them into a terrible position. I maintain these men cannot take advantage of the inducements offered by this bill. It is stated that one dollar will be given by the government for every dollar paid by the settler, but these men have no money with which to make payments. They now think it strange that the unemployed should be given 8600 without any arrangements being made for repayment. This is being done in the various provinces as a relief measure. Many of these soldier and civilian settlers would be glad to leave the land if they only knew where to go, and they would not ask for any $600.
Many of these settlers are under a greater debt to-day than they were when they took up the land originally. This is a rather serious matter. In some cases they have sold their farm in .the hope that they could obtain some recompense, but the purchasers have in many cases quit-claimed the land and so it has come back upon the original settler. The soldier settlers in British Columbia ask that all interest payments be waived for a few years. If they had any money at all they could obtain advantage under the provisions of this bill, but they have not nor have they hope of getting any. Interest charges are piling up and will pile up, and these men are asking that these interest charges be not held against them or the property. The conditions in British Columbia are entirely different from those that prevail on the prairie. I know that many of the settlers in my constituency are in a very serious plight. In many instances they assigned their cream cheques but they have been compelled to ask them back in order to live as the merchants in some instances have refused to grant them further credit. This plea is not put forward by the soldier settlers alone; it is wholeheartedly supported by all citizens. I am going to ask the minister seriously to consider this matter and see if something cannot be done to provide for the waiving of interest charges for a few years, if not for all time. I ask him also to consider the fact that in many cases the load of debt to-day is much heavier than when the original purchase was made. I just want on behalf of the settlers in my district to put on record a little matter so as to prevent misunderstanding. When the resolution on which this bill is founded, was in committee, the minister referred to a Mr. Price who, he said, was president of the Soldier Settlers' Union, and he quoted a letter Mr. Price had written on February 14. I am not quite clear that the gentleman who, I understand from those who know him, is a man of high character, is really president of a general soldier settlers' union, or rather just of the local union where he lives; at least I have before me no record, certainly not as regards British Columbia, of there being any conference of locals appointing such officers, but there may have been some more or less local arrangement. I mean no deprecation of him in that connection, but it somewhat weakens the strength of his presentation.
What I was going to say was this:	The
minister quoted a letter from Mr. Price in which the latter indicated that he would practically guarantee that the soldier settlers would keep quiet for the next five years and have no criticism to make of this policy as now brought down, if the minister put it through. There is, as I say, some misunderstanding about that, because that was on February 14, and on March 16 Mr. Price was writing-I think it is as president himself- signing himself as such, to the local in my district and taking a wholly different attitude. Instead of saying that he was satisfied with the proposed legislation such as we have it now before us, he said:
Our main objective is to secure legislation that will obtain for us a much more equitable arrangement than we are at present working under. This would, of course, include the total abolition of interest.
Further on he said:
We also made it quite clear-*
Presumably that was the conference with the minister's officials.
-that any scheme for final adjustment that did not include a total abolition of interest, would not be acceptable to us.
That does not exactly jibe with the statement he made in the letter quoted by the minister. I presume the explanation is that the letter quoted by the minister was dealing with the temporary matter of relief, whereas

this gentleman was writing to this local saying that the ultimate policy of all the unions was the total abolition of interest. I want to have it clearly understood, at least so far as the men I represent are concerned, that they are not satisfied; while they may be grateful for this temporary measure of relief, they believe it is not of a permanent character. When one is dealing with a matter like this it is not a very good thing to give merely a temporary measure of relief; it would be better to take a long view and give them something that not only would afford them hope to continue making payments, such as they may be on a reduced scale, but also allow the minister to deal with the matter finally, so that these men would know, so to speak, where they stood. There is no doubt that is their view, because I quote just a couple of lines from the local union:
The proposed act is only a form of temporary relief, which in our opinion is not the wish of the majority and which we consider will only temporarily relieve matters. In the meantime the settler has no more incentive to remain on the land than before, as private debts being unavoidably contracted now will hang over his head for years, and. providing a more permanent form of relief is not provided, we are afraid many will be forced to abandon their holdings and go on relief.
Let me say there, that is what I was speaking about a moment ago, that fear or discouragement might lead them to go off the land, whereas if they knew now they would get this further rebate, they might be encouraged to struggle along. Perhaps in five years the minister will give this relief to those who are left, but in the meantime many may become discouraged and go off the land. This man points out that he believes that is the view in the northwest also. He says also:
There is no doubt in our minds if the interest is cancelled, a large number of appointments of board officials could be cancelled with it.
That is, the overhead can be reduced. The point of view of the settlers and my point of view from my knowledge of them is that the interest should be wiped out from now on, because the government will not get it in any case, and if the government tell them now that it will be rebated, they will be encouraged to continue, whereas while it is hanging over their heads it will be a matter of discouragement ; a number will go off the land and it will only be a residue who will get relief along the line suggested. Would it not be better to say now that a permanent settlement of the situation will be made? The government from time to time have been liberal; they have made a revaluation rebate on their land and 40 per

Soldier Settlement Act
cent rebate upon their stock and so on. They have not been ungenerous; I am not charging the government with not being generous; I am dealing with the situation as it is and will be. It is sometimes the part of a wise creditor to wipe out the bigger portion of his debt and thereby be sure of getting a part of it, rather than to try to force his debtors to pay, saying: You must pay, and in the end getting nothing. That, at least, is the view of the settlers, and unless prospects change most remarkably in the next three or four years there will be no hope of the government getting this interest in any case. It would be the part of wisdom to make now whatever pronouncement they think and believe they will make ultimately. That is the view of the men I represent.

I have been told, and I believe it to be the fact, that in many instances the civilian purchaser was in a much more favoured position than the soldier purchaser, that he bought at current prices on competitive tenders, and took his chances, as it were, of getting value for his money when he purchased his farm. At any rate, the legislation of that year made no provision for the same sort of adjustment with respect to the civilian purchaser that it made with respect to the soldier,
With regard to what the hon. member for New Westminster said, comparing the treatment between the soldier settler and those whom the provinces have endeavoured to place on land, granting them each $600, if the matter is to be judged on the basis of money adjustments, the soldier settler by remedial legislation has in every case received very much more than $600. Reductions have been made by this parliament in years past amounting to almost $32,000,000. I feel certain that we all have one objective with respect to the soldier settler, and that is not to discourage him, but at the same time we must bear in mind that the people have a huge investment in these lands. I believe we are all in agreement that that course
Soldier Settlement Act

should be followed which on the one hand will ensure that the settler is ultimately able to pay for his farm and on the other that in the course of doing it the government shall not adopt any measures that will make it more difficult for the soldier. In dealing with this whole problem, which is not a simple one by any means, we must bear this in mind: Some people, both in this house and outside of it, have advocated that the soldier settler should be legislated into ownership. From what I can learn from the soldier settler himself, he does not desire that. We must also bear in mind that less than three per cent of those who went overseas are represented by the soldier settler, and many more returned soldiers went into other vocations and found themselves, and find themselves [DOT] to-day in great difficulty. So far as possible the same treatment must be given to the soldier settlers as to other soldiers who find themselves in difficult positions. I have had many communications from soldiers who went into other lines of work and became the owners of businesses that were heavily mortgaged or the owners of city homes heavily mortgaged, and who are seeking from the government, relief with respect to these debts. In principle I doubt if they are not entitled to receive the same consideration as the soldier settler. Remember, they also invested their money which was probably borrowed from friends or relatives, and many of them probably involved themselves with loan companies and banks. That class of soldier received no assistance in remedial legislation. He had to deal with a common creditor, and in many instances perhaps with the sheriff. The soldier settler, if he has fallen on evil times, at least cannot be sheriffed, if I may use the phrase, out of his farm. The soldier settler, in common with others, has had and is having a difficult time, but the course to be followed I think is to grant such relief as we can, having regard to the rights of the state in the matter, and at the same time in regard to the settler himself to encourage him not to disavow but to discharge his debt, because he has had considerable assistance by way of the legislation to which I have made reference. The principle of this bill is perhaps based on the old principle, he pays the half who does confess the debt, and this is giving him the opportunity to do it.
Reference has been made to what the Canadian Pacific has done with respect to its lands in western Canada? This bill is more than the Canadian Pacific has done. After examining the results of what the Canadian Pacific did a year ago, and having consulted with their officials charged with the ad-
ministration of those lands, I believe we shall find that many people heretofore discouraged because of the low prices for their products and for other reasons will take a great deal of encouragement from this bill. I have received scores of letters from soldier and civilian settlers in all parts of Canada, commenting upon this legislation, not all complimentary, but the great majority so, and hopeful that with this measure of assistance in the remission of interest and the credit of dollar for dollar for the period named in the bill they will, with any considerable improvement in commodity price levels, be well on their way to paying for their farms. That is the aggregate of the views I have received as a result of the communications which have been directed to me from all over Canada.
There is another aspect of the situation to which I should like to draw the attention of the committee. This bill applies with equal force all over Canada. On March 29, 1930, western Canada was particularly favoured over eastern Canada with respect to the payment of taxes; payments were made and apparently obligations assumed by what was said to be an agreement with the western provinces, in the face of advice which was then upon record, and is still there, that it was illegal to do what was being done. However I presume pressure of the times and the necessity of assisting the settler was apparent to such an extent that the government of the day thought it desirable to take such action. That action however applied only to western Canada. Why it should have been so restricted, I do not know, and there is nothing on record to indicate the reason. The legislation now before the committee, however, applies with equal force throughout Canada, and I am hopeful that the assistance here given the people on soldier settler lands combined with any considerable improvement in prices, will give that kind of encouragement which will be gratifying to every hon. member.

I thank the minister for the statement he has given, but I do not believe he has answered my question in regard to any revaluation requests of settlers with civil contracts. Suppose a request comes from a settler under a civil contract to have land revalued that he bought at S25 or S35 an acre, when the same land can now be bought for $20-and is now being offered by the soldier settlement board and the Indian department-in certain sections of northern Saskatchewan, will he consider revaluation of that land and the adjustment of the debt, if the value is greater than the debt?

settlers are told that.

I am anxious to find

How many soldiers does this amount look after?

speechtext: Something over 19,000.

I believe the minister
gave the exact figure of 19,241.

In Saskatchewan we
have a number of supervisors travelling about the country. They are able to collect only an amount which would equal the cost of maintaining them. Practically all the money they collect goes to them. It seems to me that with conditions such as now exist in western Canada we might do away with these supervisors, and that the payments due by soldiers to the government might be eliminated, or at least the interest thereon. Under present conditions in western Canada prospects of getting any money back from the soldier settlement scheme are very remote indeed. Until conditions improve my advice to the government would be to call in the supervisors and take them off the road
entirely. They are going about from one soldier settler to another, bothering and worrying them in an effort to collect money from them, when in fact the soldiers have no money to pay. They make a nuisance of themselves, and continual complaints are being made in respect to them. They are doing no good whatever, and are making trouble instead of helping.

I have some more facts
to take up in connection with this bill. I do not know whether I shall be able to complete them to-night, but I shall attempt at least to do so-to give one or more instalments, thereof. But before leaving the question of revaluation of land bought under the soldier settlement board by settlers other than soldiers, I have also a few observations to make. The minister said he would take this matter into consideration. May I impress upon him the importance of considering the matter fully? When men bought land at $30 or $35 an acre which can now be bought for $20 I think the men interested have a strong argument for some adjustment. The minister said he would consider the matter. May I impress upon him the importance of having his department give the matter the most complete consideration as quickly as possible.
Following that, may I take up with the minister one or two further points? A few days ago in the house I asked him about a complaint made by Stanley Lawrence of Huntoon, Saskatchewan, and other soldiers throughout the province. The question I put to the minister was this: I said I had received information from northern Saskatchewan that certain soldier settlers could not procure seed or feed oats. I also said these men had applied to the municipality, to the Canadian legion, to the soldier settlement board, and to the minister himself, and up to the time I received the information no action had been taken. Therefore I thought that as a member of this house from Saskatchewan I should ask the minister a straightforward question about this condition of affairs, and I did so. The minister replied the next day something like this; that the settler asked about was located not in the constituency of North Battleford, but, he thought, in the constituency of Wey-burn. I did not say that Lawrence was located in North Battleford federal riding; I said I had information regarding this complaint from northern Saskatchewan. I did not even say that the person from whom I received the information was living in the North Battleford federal riding, but I said that I had the information from that part of the province.
Soldier Settlement Act

Now the minister says this man is living in the riding of Weybum. I understand he is not living in that constituency but in the riding of Assiniboia, though under the new redistribution bill he will be in Weyburn. Of course the redistribution bill is not law yet, and in its present form may we hope it never will be. However, leaving that point aside for the moment, the information was that feed and seed oats were not got last year by this man Lawrence until June. The minister says he did get the seed in plenty of time. Lawrence says he did not. Whom are we to believe? Lawrence says he did not get the seed, did not sow it and did not reap a harvest. The minister says he got it in time. If he did not get a crop the chances are that he did not get the seed in time, and I am told Lawrence is of the opinion that the reason he did not get the seed in time was that he was a Liberal in politics and therefore was discriminated against.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Oh, nonsense.
I am not in a position to verify that statement because Lawrence is not present, but-

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
You do not believe it, I
am sure.

His own opinion was
that he did not get justice because his politics were not right. I hope he will get justice this year, because I understand he is still Liberal. I have confidence in the minister that he will not hold back seed and feed oats because the man differs politically from himself. Surely not!
But let me continue. This man applied to the municipality, to the settlement board, to the Canadian legion and to the minister, and he got no action until too late last year, and it appeared that he was not getting very quick action this year, therefore he thought the matter should be brought up in the house, and I brought it up. The minister says he has directed him what to do. Well, I am thankful to the minister, but the fact remains that up to the time the information reached here this year this man was in need of seed and had not got it. If action has been taken since I compliment the minister for setting the departmental machinery going so that this man may get the justice to which he is entitled.
Next, let me go back to the dying days of the first part of the present session. It will be remembered that last fall when the question of land settlement and soldier settlement was before the house I put a statement on Hansard, and later the minister also put a

statement on the record, saying among other things he had given to parliament all the information he could, from all over Canada. He did give a good deal of information I admit. But he said he had listened to addresses, especially from members from western Canada, which he thought would be more helpful and dependable and effective if the information had been got from the department and not from newspaper clippings and letters. Apparently the government must always have a fling at the newspapers, whether it be the weekly press or the daily. They would have us 'believe that information given to the house obtained from weekly and daily papers is often unsound information. I do not take that view at all. I believe that a government or a minister can often be put right by information got first-hand by newspapers. I think a statement of that kind was absolutely unnecessary, and would not have been required had we had in Canada a non-political unemployment advisory council for the last three years, national in character, that would have gathered all the information on soldier settlement, unemployment and land settlement generally which would have been available to any member on request. As it is now we have to dig up this information ourselves from whatever source we can get it, from letters and other first-hand information, newspapers and government departments. I believe that on the whole the information daily obtained by a member is just as authentic as anything that can be got from any department of government.
Secondly m that speech the minister said that the department of soldier settlement had been completely reorganized, and so he said it commended itself to the great majority of settlers under its control. Well I only hope that is true, but I do not think it is one hundred per cent true, indeed it is far from it. I know many soldier settlers in northern Saskatchewan feel that although the department has been reorganized it is by no means as efficient or as aggressive as it might be in ways apart from collecting money. I do not want to find fault with the present director; in fact I would like to encourage him, and in turn ask him to encourage the men on the land-the soldier settlers. But the fact that the department has been reorganized is no proof that there are not grievances which ought to be adjusted as completely and as quickly as possible.
Thirdly, the minister further made certain criticisms of myself,-and I am not finding any fault; it was ligitimate criticism and I do not mind anyone criticizing me so long as the
criticism appears sound. I had occasion in that

Soldier Settlement Act
address in the house to put on record a report of a meeting at Medstead, Saskatchewan, in connection with land settlement. The settlers concerned received S600 a year, $200 from the municipality, $200 from the province and $200 from this government, and some of these were soldier settlers. A meeting was arranged at which four or five municipalities were represented. I was invited to that meeting, and I thought it only right that, as a member, I should attend. The meeting was attended by thirty or forty reeves, secretaries, and councillors. As far as the meeting was concerned I put on record a very straightforward statement about the existing condition of affairs in northern Saskatchewan in regard to soldier settlement and land settlement generally. When the minister discovered that that report had been published in my own paper, the North Battleford News, that I had personally attended the meeting, that I had written the report myself and that it appeared in the North Battleford News, controlled by myself, he suggested that the statements could not be proven in that way. That, I submit, is a lame argument; it is about the least plausible argument anyone would wish to hear. If a report appears in a newspaper, weekly or daily, owned by a certain individual, that report being written by the owner of the newspaper, is it more authentic or less authentic then a report written by someone acting simply as a reporter? Any schoolboy would answer immediately that the report of a meeting, written by the owner of a newspaper, a meeting attended by the owner himself and at which he heard every speech delivered, every statement made, every argument iput forward touching the question at issue-in this instance the land settlement scheme-would be an absolutely authentic report, a report much more authentic than one written by some person without any interest in the paper and without considering anything apart from a mechanical report of the proceedings. I would say there was no proof necessary. The facts were self evident, and although they were stated in the North Battleford News they were not written to prove anything but to give information to all who wanted to learn.
Will the hon. member be good enough to stick to the point?

I am sticking to the point, and I am not going to take up very much of the time of the committee. If this matter cannot be fully discussed now, Mr. Chairman, then it will have to be discussed 53719-298
on the third reading, so that it does not make much difference. May I say, then, that one . of the reeves present at that meeting said that in his district there would be no crop and no cash. How then could a soldier pay for land without either crop or cash?
Surely the hon. member must know that his remarks are not relevant to the section under consideration.
We have not been confining ourselves to one section, Mr. Chairman.
We are discussing section 72.
I introduced my remarks under section 72.
I trust the hon. gentleman will use his good judgment and not wander too far.

I submit that my remarks are relevant, Mr. Chairman. Another reeve, Mr. Comerford, said that settlers had been dumped into his area of the country and that fifty schooi children were without school accommodation. These soldier settlers were also in a hopeless situation. The reeve of Medstead, Mr. Soderberg. said that the land the soldiers were put on was hopeless and that it would be impossible for them to succeed. Perhaps I had better give briefly the statements of one or two of these men. Mr. Grimes, the reeve of Parkdale, pointed out clearly that the costs were piling up against these men. They were supposed to pay their taxes but could not; they were supposed to pay for hospitalization but could not; they were supposed to pay for medical attention, and that was impossible. They had no money with which to discharge any of these obligations, and as a consequence the department at Regina requested the reeve and secretary of the latter municipality to interview each settler, and report, which they refused to do. Taking all the circumstances into consideration, I would say that the report placed on Hansard was informative; it did not require to be proven because as I have said, it was self evident, and it was essential that that information should be given to parliament and the country.
With regard to another question which the minister dealt with, he said that the Soldier Settlers' Union sent out an alarming circular, and that these soldier settlers wanted to put something across.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
I did not say that.

Soldier Settlement Act

These are the minister's words:
An organization was formed there among the soldier settlers; they communicated with me and sent out rather an alarming circular as to what attitude they intended to adopt with respect to discharging their obligations to the crown. But when they met, there apparently was sound sense among most of the settlers, and those who organized the union were not able to put across the sentiments expressed in the circular.
I do not think there is anything alarming in the circular. I have the circular here and I cannot see for the life of me why the minister characterized as alarming the actions of the men who organized the Soldier Settlers' Union in Saskatchewan, nor do I understand why he should suggest that they were trying to put something across. I for one certainly do not believe that they were trying to put across anything but what was right. I know personally the secretary, Major H. F. Packman, and the secretary, Lieutenant-Colonel H. J. Price.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Mr. Packman was one of the representatives at the meeting when these amendments were discussed-
I understand that.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: -and he approved of them and abandoned the proposition set out in the circular.

Here are some of the points with which the organization dealt in that circular, and I will leave it to the minister to say which of them are alarming and which are not. We may have a difference of opinion about what is alarming. I hope we have.
So do I.

I am glad the hon. gentleman has some opinions-also hopes. First of all, the chairman says that the organization is non-politicail. That should suit the minister. Further, the statement is made that the organization has been formed for the sole purpose of enabling all soldier settlers to get together. Let me quote precisely what is said:
The Soldier Settlers' Union is a non-political organization, which has been formed for the sole purpose of enabling all soldier settlers to get together as a strong, united body, so that we may be able to demand and obtain justice and common sense in the administration of our affairs by the soldier settlement board.
Is there anything wrong with that? Where is the alarming sentiment? There is nothing whatever alarming in that statement. Take the next:
For years there has been a growing feeling of dissatisfaction amongst soldier settlers, both

at the terms of our contracts and at the treatment accorded us by the board. This has culminated, in Lloydminster district, in the formation of the union.
In other words, the organization of the Soldier Settlers' Union came about as a result of the dissatisfaction that existed between the soldier settlers and the soldier settlement board; because there was that dissatisfaction, because of unsatisfactory treatment, these men made up their minds to organize. I should like to know what is wrong about any body of men organizing when they have a grievance. Are not assembly and organization two of the fundamentals of what we might term British liberty? I think so. If we have not the right to organize when we have a grievance, then we have no democracy that is worth while. If we cannot assemble to state our grievance, what freedom do we enjoy? None whatever. I say therefore that there is nothing alarming in that statement. Let me quote the third:
Our farms were purchased at highly inflated prices, and in spite of some reduction and concessions made by the government, the amount still owing on them is, in the majority of cases, out of all proportion to their earning power.
That is true, and if it is, even though it is a little alarming, what is wrong with it? Nothing at all so far as I. can see. It is a perfectly justifiable statement by men who are anxious to improve their position. Take the next:
- It is realized by most of us that it is impossible for us to repay our loans, as they now stand. We are steadily going behind, and piling up a debt of principal and interest, which we can never hope to liquidate.
They are going behind and they do not hope to be ever able to pay up. This is what they tell the minister in this circular, and the minister describes it as alarming. Well, it may be alarming to the department, but the sooner some action is taken by the department to allay that discontent the better. Statement number 5 reads:
This situation is due to no fault of ours, and exists in spite of every effort we have made to dear off our liabilities to the board.
They have done their best but they have gone behind and cannot pay up. They told that to the board, and the minister now says that that was an alarming statement. There is no question about it, it is a statement of fact and if it is alarming, all the more reason why the department should take action. The next statement reads:
Although our present position is obviously due to factors over which we have no control, the government insists that we shall repay our loans in full.

Soldier Settlement Act
Listen to that! They have made their complaints to the department and they have been told that they must repay their loans in full. They were told at that time, which was August 20, 1932, there would be no hope of any concessions or adjustments held out, they would have to pay the principal and pay the interest. If they did not do that, more than likely they would be evicted.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I know the hon. member would not consciously make a statement-
I would not make a statement which I could not back up.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: -not in accordance with the facts. I think I stated before that the seizures all over Canada were less than three-tenths of one per cent. These seizures were not evictions in any sense of the word, and in no case was there justification for the attitude taken by the settlers. I am absolutely certain that the action taken by the department in the very small number of cases was the correct action under the circumstances. I believe that that action was proper and I believe it would have been taken by every hon. member of this committee under similar circumstances. The statement has been made by the hon. member with respect to evictions taking place if payment was not made, but that has not been the policy of the government since this depression commenced. The soldier settlers knew that and I think they have done very well considering the difficulties which have confronted them in common with all others in almost every walk of life.

My statement was that
the thought present in the minds of these soldier settlers was that if they did not pay up in full, in all probability they would be evicted. I did not say that that was the policy of the department.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: There was no reason for any such fear.

If the minister will
listen for a little while I think I can show him that there was a foundation for such a fear. It was because of that fear that these men organized. They satisfied themselves that the quicker they got organized, the better for themselves.
The next statement made in the circular is to the effect that they had received every reasonable reduction and concession from the government and need expect no further help from that source. That is, they got every desirable concession and reduction. They felt that if the information they got that day was correct, then they had no great reason to expect any further reductions or concessions.

That was the reason they organized. The next statement has some bearing upon the eviction question. The minister should listen. It reads:
It was made perfectly clear by these officials that the policy of the board would be to demand full payment of our loans, and that in the event of our failure to meet the payments from any cause whatsoever, eviction proceedings would be taken.
That is the statement made by the secretary of the Soldiers Settlers' Union who writes this circular.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
When this circular first
came to my attention I read it over carefully and made inquiry with reference to that particular paragraph. I can assure the hon. member that no such statement was ever made by any official of the department. If such a statement had been made at that meeting, does the hon. member think for one moment that the department would not have been deluged by letters and telegrams? Of course that would have happened, but we never heard a word of it until we received this circular. I am absolutely satisfied that the party responsible for the printing of this circular, perhaps not by design but certainly in some way or another, has included a statement which is absolutely in contradiction of the facts. I made certain that no such statement had been made.

I will take the word of the minister and the officials of his department. I want to take the word of the minister that eviction proceedings were not in his mind or in the minds of his officials. I am very glad to receive that information but my point still stands that the feeling which prompted these men to organize was that if they did not get busy and organize to protect themselves-as organization always does-they would more than likely be evicted. Another statement reads:
It would be well for every soldier settler to clearly understand the situation. Unless some means is adopted of changing the present policy of the government, we must pay up our loans in full-an obvious impossibility-or eventually lose our farms.
That statement amplifies the idea of eviction. As the result of that feeling, the soldier settlers organized.
When they organized they had two objectives. The first objective was the finding of a solution for the problem which confronted them last fall. That was their immediate objective.	They wanted to find out how
they could stay on the land and how they could keep themselves from being evicted. But their main objective was one which brings us more closely to the provisions
Soldier Settlement Act

of this bill. They asked for a better and more equitable deal for all soldier settlers. This legislation attempts to meet that objective in a modified form. The soldier settlers feel that if they cannot get a new deal they will never be able to pay off their loans and will never be free from the threat of eviction. As this circular states, that threat is constantly before them. There is another statement made in the circular which should be put on the record. I want to be fair to the department, so I will quote this statement along with the others. It is stated that the feeling was that as soon as grain prices went up these collectors would be on their backs again with more fury than ever, dragooning them to pay the last cent of their obligations. That is followed with the thought that the more thoroughly they are organized, the less unreasonable will be the demands they will have to meet. They state quite plainly that they want to meet their obligations. They want to remain on their farms if it is at all possible, and they do not want to cheat the government out of one cent. These are some of the facts in connection with the organization of the Soldier Settlers' Union as found in the preliminary statement of the secretary.
I stated before in my address that there was a certain soldier settler, A. J. Sibley, living over ten miles out of North Battle-ford. This man had a grievance. As the minister said, officials from Saskatoon were sent to visit that man. On their way to visit him they called at my home and they asked me to go out with them. I went along with them to see what was going on. These officials had an interview with Mr. Sibley that day; they came to a certain understanding; they left and I returned with them. Because I did this, the minister put it on record in a very improper manner. Fancy a 'minister of the crown putting stuff like this on Hansard! This is what he said:
The superintendent took him-
That is myself.
-right down to that settler and let him investigate the condition for himself.
I did not investigate the condition.

speechtext:
What did the hon. member
do?
Mr. MoINTOSH: The superintendent from Saskatoon went out and investigated. The only reason I went with the minister's officials from Saskatoon was that I was asked to go and that if my presence could be of any help in any way to get the two parties together, I was willing to go. I did not even hear or want to hear what was said; I do not
r\Ir. McIntosh.}
know what their understanding or agreement was. Yet the minister makes this statement in the house:
He knew the arrangement at that time-
I certainly did not know the arrangement.
-and after seeing the condition for himself he drove home with the superintendent and did not have a single word of criticism to offer.
Then he says that after not having a word of criticism to offer, I came to Ottawa and placed critical statements on the record of the house.

The hon. member
certainly did.

I certainly did place proper criticisms on Hansard, and, if necessary, I will do so again. Such a statement by the minister is absolutely unfair; that report is a departmentally coloured one and not worth the ink with/which it is written. speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
What statement?
Mr. MoINTOSH: The statement I have just referred to. Let me go a step further. Further on the minister says that statements made by myself and other western members in connection with soldier settlement were really breaking down the financial structure of Canada; that men who had invested in western bonds, sold them and bade good-bye to Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba as investment areas. I can only say this, that if telling the truth and putting on record the grievances of our soldier settlers who fought in the war to win liberty and who are entitled to redress, will scare away from western Canada some superficial investors, the quicker they are scared out of western Canada the better. So far as I am concerned, I am going to put on record statements of that kind just when I feel they ought to be made public. I do not think by putting them on record, we interfere with western development; in fact I think, by putting these facts on record and telling the truth about western Canada, we help western development.

The hon. gentleman's time is up.
