Yes, forty minutes.
Well, I shall have something to say a little later on.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: If we could get on with this bill, all this discussion can and, I think, probably will take .place when the estimates of this department come before the house later on. I would like, if possible, to advance this bill because I want to take the necessary course the legislation contemplates to take care of the various soldiers' accounts and settlers' accounts that will have to be adjusted in conformity with the legislation.
Well, I can put on record the rest of my information on the third reading of the bill, if necessary; I do not want to delay the minister too long to-night.

The hon. member for
North Battleford has raised the question of seed and feed oats for the settlers. I understand there is no seed and feed oats being put out by the government. When I have been approached, I have given that information. There is one thing in this bill to which I should like to refer, and that is in regard to the interest that is being cancelled. I am sorry that it is being cancelled for only one year. The hard years of 1929-30, 1930-31 and 1931-32, as the minister well knows, have been the most difficult years for the settler and I regret very much that this legislation has not been drawn so that more interest could be cancelled than for the one year. I suppose the minister would not consider an amendment at this time, but although there is a great deal of good in the bill, it would have been more acceptable if the government had been able to cancel more than the interest for one year.

I presume I can now
speak for another forty minutes, if necessary, but I do not expect to do so. I believe it is better to put on record now the remainder of what I want to say on this bill; it will be more connected.
Coming now to the bill that is before the committee, may I refer to the meeting that took place in Saskatoon when the president and secretary of the soldier settlement union and other representative soldier settlers convened in that city and, I understand, met the soldier settlement director. A general discussion took place about the complaints that I have put on Hansard, and as to what ought and should be done, otherwise these men
would lose their farms. In other words, these men had to have a new understanding with the department and they were out to have it. The department very kindly arranged a meeting which was held in Saskatoon, as I said, and a veiy free and full discussion took place in regard to soldier settlement questions. What transpired at that meeting? Well, the memorandum that was presented at the meeting bjT the soldier settlers was made up of eight points which bore entirely on the problems of the soldier settlers in the prairie provinces.
The first was that because of unprecedented low price levels of agricultural products, coupled with drought, soldier settlers have been operating at serious loss during the past three years. They were not paying operating expenses because of the low price level of agriculture products and because of the serious drought in western Canada. That was one point which they put in the memorandum.
The second was: The accumulation of debts was so great that the average settler would be unable to overtake his liability even with the return of normal times.
As soon as normal times return and price levels would rise, the soldier settlers felt the}' would be called upon to make payments they could not make and therefore they were very anxious to bring this important aspect of the question before the department. They made the statement that even with the return of normal times, they were quite hopeless about overtaking their liabilities.
The third point was: As a result of these conditions surrounding soldier settlers, discouragement, hopelessness, a lowering of their morale and a loss of their incentive to work had been brought about. Because they were losing their morale and their initiative, becoming hopeless and discouraged, they welcomed the opportunity of laying their whole case before the department at Saskatoon.
Now for number 4. The soldier settlers agree among themselves that to carry on with any assurance of ultimate success some adjustment of debt is necessary in order to remove anxiety and uphold their faith in the future.
If they are going to carry on there must be a remission of interest from the government and there must be some debt readjustment. Paving the way for this bill, Mr. Chairman, for a bill which a few months before they were told would not be brought down because the department had given the soldier settlers to understand that they would have to pay the last cent and that no action would be taken by the department.

Soldier Settlement Act

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I have already said that no such statement was made a few months previously.

I will accept the minister's word, but the soldier settlers got that idea, and I understand that they got it at the organization meeting, and that they were told that. I am not to blame. I am merely putting on record the facts of the case.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Might I interrupt again, because I am afraid there is going to be a misconception, whether it is of importance or not. I have a copy of the minutes of the meeting covering all these points, and I find that what the hon. member is referring to was not presented to the meeting at all. It was after the discussion at the meeting that this memorandum of these various points was drawn up and subscribed to by everybody present at the meeting including the director himself, who assisted in the preparation of what the hon. member is reading from, and it was upon this memorandum together with subsequent conferences that the present legislation was founded.

Exactly what I am coming to if the minister would allow me to do it.
Number 5 says that the soldier settlers keenly appreciate the concessions already made -on their behalf but these concessions were necessitated not merely because of the inability of the settler to meet his obligations but because of the fundamental defects of the soldier settler scheme which made it impossible for the soldier settler to farm profitably enough to make his payments.
That is a very fair statement, and it entered into the discussions later.
Number 6. It was realized that the soldier settler could not reasonably expect to receive concessions simply as a soldier settler.
That is quite fair, Mr. Chairman, Number 6 continues:
But since the provincial governments are taking steps to relieve the debt burden of the civilian population it was thought the Dominion government, as the authority to adjust soldier settlement schemes, should also effect a general measure of debt adjustment on behalf of soldier settlers.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I must ask the hon. member to permit me to interject again. I am following the certified copy of the report of the meeting, and number 6-there has been some subsection from other topics-

I am giving just the
essence of each part of the memorandum.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Number 6 has been emasculated beyond all recognition.

No, I am coming to that if the minister will allow me. He is in too much of a hurry.
Number 7. Any relief suggested should be devised on an absolutely equitable basis, and not framed to help the improvident. Only in this way can the soldier settlers secure maximum returns at minimum of expense.
The last statement in their memorandum was to the effect that the question of a free grant was discussed, and the soldier settlers said in conference that they did not favour it. The soldier settlers went on record as being desirous of paying for their farms. I have made that statement before, but may I say to the minister that I believe that on the whole the sentiments among the soldier settlers are to the effect that they cannot pay for their farms. They say so. They say that even with a return to normaJl prices they feel they will be unable to overtake their liabilities. If that is the case I echo the sentiments expressed here to-night by other members from western Canada, that if the soldier settlers cannot pay for their farms, then instead of keeping a certain number of officials in their positions and in the collection field, the quicker something eminently satisfactory is done the better.
May I also say to the minister that if the department demands payment in full, the feeling among the soldier settlers is that the payments could be made just as well to any postmaster in the district, to be forwarded by him to the department. The soldier settlers urge that if that can be done, it should be done, and then these men who are covering the country in their cars, using up cars and gasoline and costing the nation a great deal of money, can be taken off and the soldier settlers can make their payments to some body like the Post Office Department, and the money be forwarded to the soldier settlement department. It would save a great deal of expense, and it would have the effect of giving the soldiers a different feeling towards the department from what they harm at the present time.
In conclusion, as the minister said, after this memorandum was presented to the meeting certain action was taken and the point of view of the soldier settlers was given very emphatically. One point of view was this, that there should be a total abolition of interest retroactive to 1929, and that any interest payments that should be made should apply on the amortized debt, that is on the

principal plus the interest up to 1929. By this bill only one year's interest is taken off the debt of the soldier settlers-1931 to 1932.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Is my hon. friend still reading from the same minutes of the same meeting?
Yes, the same meeting.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I have a certified copy here and it is entirely different.
This must be all right because it is in your bill only you have not gone far enough.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
The recommendation with respect to interest is clear and cannot be misunderstood :
That the interest on outstanding loans for the year 1932 should be remitted, and in any case in which any settler has already paid his interest that payment should be applied on his principal debt.
That is signed by my hon. friend's friends, including Colonel Harry Price, Mr. Packman, General Ross of Yorkton and all the representatives that attended the meeting, and the recommendation was unanimously carried. So that the record will not be hopelessly confused and uninteresting to anyone who wants the facts, I would earnestly suggest that my hon. friend should stick to what the minutes of the meeting say.

Here is the statement
I have here, Number 1, the same as the minister is reading from, and it is exactly as I have given it, only I have given it in a briefer way.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
You have gone back to
1929.

The statement is this:
Total abolition of interest retroactive to 1929, also any interest payment made to apply on principal debt.
Now I understand that the soldier settler wants a total abolition of interest from the year 1929. This bill eliminates only one year's interest, and therefore it is not satisfactory. More than that, I believe that the wish of the soldier settlers is that no more interest be paid on these debts, and the reason simply is that the soldier settlers figure they cannot pay it. That is why they want the interest clause in this bill retroactive to 1929. That is where the bill falls short. I would like to see the bill amended to provide for the total abolition of interest not only back to 1929 but forward through the years, so that these men will be given at least a fair chance
Soldier Settlement Act
to pay their obligations. Otherwise they say they cannot pay, and it is hopeless to expect any interest.	_
Now, number 2, and I am coming to the clause you are so anxious about, Mr. Chairman, and that is the double credit clause, by which if a man pays one dollar he gets credit for two dollars, and this is to go on for four years. May I compliment the minister and his department for making this for a period of four years? I am not anxious to find fault with the minister or his department. I wish merely to place the facts on Hansard so that they may be recorded on behalf of these men who feel that they ought to have someone in the House of Commons -in fact, many members-speak on their behalf. The clause of the bill which gives a double credit for four years was debated at the conference. I believe the wish of the director, who is present with us to-night, was to make it active for two years. Now in the bill it has been made four years, or just double the suggestion made at the meeting.
I congratulate the minister upon taking new ground, and going forward. I like to see people go forward, and in the formation of legislation I like to see departments go ahead. Therefore in that regard the extension of the double credit for four years is, in my view, a sound part of the bill, and will be satisfactory to soldier settlers.
Lastly, the lien on equipment was released. Again I believe this is a sound step in advance, and I thank the minister and his department for taking it. In 1930 the lien was taken off stock. In this bill we are making null and void any lien on equipment, and by doing so I believe we will be helping the soldier settlers.
In closing may I ask the minister to consider very carefully one of the outstanding points in connection with help to soldier settlers, namely the total abolition of interest retroactive to 1929, with provision for no more interest payments in the future. Secondly, I recommend that full consideration be given to the problems of soldier settlers generally, so that if the soldiers cannot pay for their land, something constructive be done to leave them in possession of their property, or, better still, hand their farms back to them free of all encumbrances. If the government will adopt these suggestions perhaps some of the ill-advised expenses now obtaining in connection with staffs collecting moneys from soldier settlers and selling their crops-all but a third, when debts are not paid up to the minute- might be eliminated. When soldier settlers feel it is impossible to pay any more than they are paying, and when officers have not other
Soldier Settlement Act

work to do, but pester the life out of them to pay! pay! the government would do well to call off these highly paid collecting officials and have soldier settler problems more constructively and economically dealt with.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On subsection 73-Additional credit on payments of arrears of instalments.

I should like to ask a question which may have been asked before in an earlier part of the discussion, respecting the relief from interest payments of purchasers from settlers. Supposing a civilian purchased from a soldier settler, what would be the arrangement with respect to interest? As I understand it under this legislation he would receive the same relief as the soldier settler' would have received. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Yes.

Carrying out that idea, I suggest we should go farther and define the term "settler." In the explanatory notes I find the expression "any settler or purchaser." But in the bill are the words "any settler or person." In the interpretation clause we find that "settler" is defined as:
A person who at any time during the war has been therein engaged on active service in a military force.
Then various conditions are given.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: That is the reason it is so worded in section 73 of the bill.

Apparently the words "or person" are used but I suggest they are capable of a dangerous interpretation. I would certainly appreciate it if the expression "any settler or civilian purchaser" were used. But when we come to the word "person" we are confronted with the argument that a settler is a person. Is there anywhere in the act a definition of what a person is? It might be argued that a person eventually means a settler, and a settler means a man who has been in active service. The wording may create very great hardship, if there be any doubt as to the application to a civilian purchaser. I do not believe any harm would be done by making a change, even if it were only to allay apprehensions of possible difficulty. I recall a few years ago that on a bill similar to this one I asked the minister then at the head of the department a question in connection with revaluation, as to whether so and so would mean so and so, and I was told most emphatically that it would. The 
minister's answer appeared in Plansard. Six months later the department absolutely repudiated the assurance I had been given by the minister, and said they were not bound by it. As a result a number of people suffered an injustice. When we come to interpretation, we cannot go by what someone may say; we must take what is expressed. If the minister could see his way clear to put in the words "or civilian purchaser" he would relieve the minds of a good many people, and I believe would be doing no harm to anybody.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
That very point was in
contemplation when the bill was drawn. From a purely legal standpoint I gave it consideration. In order that there might be no doubt that the word "person" would cover people other than settlers as interpreted in the act, I submitted the section to the officers of the Department of Justice, and their judgment was that the words now appearing amply covered all others indebted under the act, because a settler is interpreted to mean as the hon. member for Comox-Alberni has read from the act. Other persons not being settlers who have purchased under the act are taken care of by the language appearing in the first line of the section.
But you do not say "persons other than settlers."

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
I do not know how we
can make it any clearer than we have. "Civilian purchaser" would confuse the issue.

You could say "settler or
person other than a settler." How would that do? Then, would the word "arrears" in the twenty-second line of the bill cover a payment made by the government for taxes? Would that come under the things for which he could get a dollar for dollar rebate?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Yes, taxes paid prior would come under the operation of the statute.

Could the minister use the
language "or person other than settler'?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
I should like to defer to
the judgment of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, but as a lawyer I say we are using the broadest possible term we can use. I have submitted the matter to the law officers of the crown and they agree with me. I very much fear if we used any other expression we would be more likely to contract than to expand the meaning.
Very well; you are a lawyer.

In subsection 2 I
find the words:
No such additional credit shall be accorded in respect of moneys the proceeds of alienation of any property charged under this act or of fire insurance.
And so on. Then in the explanatory clause on the opposite page I find the following:
Moneys received from the disposal of the department's security and credited to the account of the settler or purchaser will not be augmented by the bonus.
Will the bonus be granted to the present occupant of the land under one of those tripartite agreements?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Yes.

Then in the case of an agreement that is about paid up, if the purchaser under one of those agreements makes the final payment or close to the final payment, he will get a credit of an equal amount, and that will be lessening the equity that the soldier setter had, will it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: No I do not think it lessens his equity.

Suppose the balance
owing on a contract was S500; the soldier settler has an equity in that land of $250. The purchaser pays $250 and gets credit for $500. The $250 would wipe out the equity that the soldier settler himself had in the tripartite agreement?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: No, I think the hon. member has a misconception. It would not disturb the equity of the soldier settler at all. The civilian purchaser, if we so call him, would be credited dollar for dollar of the amount he owed1 the department. It would not destroy or affect any equity that the soldier settler has in the land. I am confident that that is the interpretation.

I doubt whether the
minister is correct in that, or whether he understood the question I put. When it comes to the final payment it seems to me that all that civilian settler needs to pay is one-half the amount, and he gets credit for the other half. That other half may be a part of the soldier settler's equity. It seems to me some change should be made in this section to take care of such cases.
